blocks.html: In Earth Science you met air pressure as the push of the air around us. Physics gives that push a number: pressure is force spread over an area, $P = F/A$, measured in pascals (Pa), one newton on each square meter. This lesson puts real numbers on the air's push and sorts out the units that weather reports use.

Air pressure at a place is the weight of the whole column of air above each square meter. At sea level it averages $101{,}325$ Pa, which weather maps write as $1013.25$ hPa (hectopascals). One hectopascal is 100 Pa, the same as one millibar (mb). U.S. reports use inches of mercury: $1\ \text{inHg} = 33.86$ hPa, so the average is $29.92$ inHg.

Picture a square meter of beach and the column of air standing on it, all the way to the top of the atmosphere. That column holds about 10,300 kg of air. Its weight, about $10{,}300 \times 9.8 \approx 101{,}000$ N, rests on one square meter: about $101{,}000$ Pa. Air is a fluid, and its molecules hit surfaces from every side, so this push acts sideways and upward as well as down. That is why the air under a table pushes up as hard as the air above pushes down, and why your body, with fluids inside pushing back, is not crushed.

blocks.html: A mercury barometer is a glass tube, closed at the top, standing in a dish of mercury. The air pushes on the dish and holds up a column of mercury whose weight per area matches the air's push: about 760 mm (29.92 inches) at sea level. Mercury is used because it is dense (13.6 times as dense as water); a water barometer would need a tube about 10.3 m tall. Most barometers today are aneroid: a sealed metal capsule that flexes as the pressure changes.

blocks.title: From inches to hectopascals
blocks.q: A TV forecast gives the pressure as 30.12 inHg. What is that in hectopascals?
steps: Each inch of mercury is 33.86 hPa: $30.12\ \text{inHg} \times 33.86\ \dfrac{\text{hPa}}{\text{inHg}}$.
The inHg units cancel, as with any unit fraction: $= 1019.9$ hPa.
That is about 7 hPa above the average: fairly high pressure.

blocks.title: How much air is above you?
blocks.q: Sea-level pressure is 101,325 Pa. What mass of air stands on each square meter? Use $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
steps: The force on 1 m² is $F = PA = 101{,}325\ \text{Pa} \times 1\ \text{m}^2 = 101{,}325$ N.
That force is the column's weight, $mg$, so $m = F/g = 101{,}325 \div 9.8$.
$m \approx 10{,}340$ kg: more than ten tonnes of air on every square meter.

blocks.html: Thinking a barometer weighs the air in the room. A barometer in a closed room reads the same as one just outside the window, because the room's air is pressed by the whole column above the building. It measures the weight of the whole column of air overhead, which is why it reads less on a mountain, where part of the column is below you. Check: an answer near 1000 hPa (or 30 inHg) is about one atmosphere's worth.
Millibars and hectopascals are the same size, so 1008 mb is 1008 hPa. Forecasters switched to the name hectopascal to match the SI unit, the pascal.

blocks.html: Drive up a mountain or take off in a plane and your ears pop: the pressure outside has dropped. Pressure is the weight of the air above you (measuring air pressure), so every meter you climb leaves some air below. The question is how fast it falls, and the answer is not a straight line.

Air can be squeezed. The air near the ground carries the weight of all the air above it, so it is packed the most tightly. Climb the first kilometer and you pass through thick, dense air and lose about 12% of the pressure. A kilometer higher, the air is thinner, so you pass less mass and lose fewer hectopascals, but still about 12% of what is left. Losing the same fraction for each step is exponential decay, just like a 12% discount taken again and again.

Pressure falls by about half for every 5.5 km you climb: $$P \approx P_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{z/5.5\ \text{km}}$$ About half of the air is below 5.5 km, three quarters below 11 km, and seven eighths below 16.5 km.

blocks.name: es-atmosphere
blocks.cap: Temperature (left) and pressure (right) up to 120 km. Drag the probe: at 5.5 km the pressure is about half of the ground's, at 11 km about a quarter. The pressure curve bends; it is not a straight line.

blocks.title: Two halvings
blocks.q: The pressure at the ground is 1012 hPa. About what is the pressure at 11 km, where airliners cruise?
steps: 11 km is two steps of 5.5 km, so the pressure halves twice.
$506 \div 2 = 253$ hPa at 11 km.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: A weather balloon reads 125 hPa when the ground reads 1000 hPa. About how high is it?
steps: $1000 \div 125 = 8$, and $8 = 2^3$: the pressure has halved three times.
Each halving is 5.5 km, so the height is $3 \times 5.5 = 16.5$ km.

blocks.title: The first kilometer versus a higher one
blocks.q: Starting from 1000 hPa, each kilometer keeps about 0.882 of the pressure below it. Compare the drop across the first kilometer with the drop from 5 km to 6 km.
steps: First kilometer: $1000 \times 0.882 = 882$ hPa, a drop of about 118 hPa.
At 5 km: $1000 \times 0.882^5 \approx 533$ hPa; at 6 km: $533 \times 0.882 \approx 470$ hPa.
That drop is only about 63 hPa: the same fraction of a smaller amount.

blocks.html: Treating the fall as a straight line: "1013 hPa drops about 500 hPa in the first 5.5 km, so by 11 km the pressure is zero." Each 5.5 km takes away half of what is left, so 11 km still has about a quarter. Check: pressure never reaches zero on this rule; it keeps halving.

blocks.html: In chemistry you used the combined gas law, $P_1V_1/T_1 = P_2V_2/T_2$, for a fixed amount of gas in a container. The atmosphere has no container, so meteorologists write the same law with density (mass per volume) in place of volume. It ties together pressure, temperature and density, three things a weather balloon measures, and it explains why warm air rises.
For air, $$P = \rho R T$$ with $P$ in pascals, density $\rho$ in kg/m³, temperature $T$ in kelvins and $R = 287$ J/(kg·K) for dry air. At the same pressure, warmer air is less dense than colder air.

Start from the ideal gas law, $PV = nR^*T$, where $R^* = 8.314$ J/(mol·K). The number of moles is the mass divided by the mass of one mole: $n = m/M$, and a mole of dry air has a mass of $M = 0.02897$ kg. So $P = \dfrac{m}{V}\cdot\dfrac{R^*}{M}\,T = \rho\,RT$, with $R = 8.314 \div 0.02897 \approx 287$ J/(kg·K). The temperature must be absolute because pressure comes from molecules hitting surfaces, and their energy of motion is proportional to the kelvin temperature: at 0 K they would not move at all.

blocks.title: Air at sea level
blocks.q: Find the density of air at 101,325 Pa and 15 °C.
steps: Convert to kelvins (temperature scales): $T = 15 + 273.15 = 288.15$ K.
Solve $P = \rho R T$ for density: $\rho = \dfrac{P}{RT} = \dfrac{101{,}325}{287 \times 288.15}$.
$\rho \approx 1.225$ kg/m³: a cubic meter of air has a mass of about 1.2 kg.

blocks.title: Warm air and cold air
blocks.q: At 1000 hPa (100,000 Pa), compare the density of air at 35 °C with air at −5 °C.
steps: Warm air: $T = 308.15$ K, so $\rho = 100{,}000 \div (287 \times 308.15) \approx 1.131$ kg/m³.
Cold air: $T = 268.15$ K, so $\rho = 100{,}000 \div (287 \times 268.15) \approx 1.299$ kg/m³.
At the same pressure, $\rho$ is proportional to $1/T$, so the ratio is $308.15/268.15 \approx 1.15$: the cold air is about 15% denser.
blocks.a: Warm air 1.13 kg/m³, cold air 1.30 kg/m³

blocks.title: Finding the pressure
blocks.q: A balloon measures air at −20 °C with a density of 0.70 kg/m³. What is the pressure?
steps: $P = \rho R T = 0.70 \times 287 \times 253.15 \approx 50{,}860$ Pa.
That is about 509 hPa, so the balloon is near 5.5 km, where pressure has halved.

blocks.html: Putting Celsius into the gas law. With $T = -5$ in the formula, a cold day would give air a negative density, and 0 °C would divide by zero. Always add 273.15 first. Check: for air near the ground, $T$ should be roughly 230 to 320 K, and the density about 1 to 1.4 kg/m³.

blocks.name: es-atmosphere
blocks.cap: Move the probe and read the air density tile. At 5.5 km the density is about 0.70 kg/m³, a bit more than half of the ground's, because the air there is also colder.

blocks.html: This is why warm air rises. A bubble of air warmer than its surroundings, at the same pressure, is less dense, so the denser air around it pushes it up, the way water pushes up a cork. Heat a pocket of air by 3 °C and it becomes about 1% less dense: enough to float upward. Try it in Gas in a Box: heat the box and watch the pressure climb, then let it expand and watch the gas spread out.

blocks.html: In Earth Science you saw the greenhouse effect as a story: sunlight comes in, heat goes out, and some gases catch part of the heat. This unit puts numbers on that story, starting with a fact from astronomy: hotter things glow at shorter wavelengths. The Sun and Earth glow very differently, and that difference is the key to the whole energy balance.

Everything warmer than absolute zero gives off electromagnetic radiation. Its brightest wavelength follows Wien's law: $$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2898\ \mu\text{m·K}}{T}$$ The Sun (about 5772 K) peaks near 0.5 μm, in visible light. Earth (about 288 K) peaks near 10 μm, in the infrared.

A warm object glows because its molecules and electrons jiggle, and jiggling charges send out light. Hotter matter jiggles faster and more violently, so it sends out more of the short, energetic waves. That is why a stove ring goes from dull red to orange as it heats, and why a star's color tells its temperature. Cooler things still glow; they just glow at wavelengths too long for our eyes. Astronomers write the same law in nanometers: $2.898 \times 10^6$ nm·K is the same constant as 2898 μm·K.

blocks.name: es-energy
blocks.cap: The glow of the Sun and of Earth (each scaled to fit). Sunlight peaks in the visible band; Earth's glow peaks near 10 μm. The shaded bands are where water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb Earth's infrared; most sunlight passes through.

blocks.title: The Sun's peak
blocks.q: The Sun's surface is about 5772 K. At what wavelength does its glow peak?
steps: $\lambda_{\text{peak}} = 2898 \div 5772$ μm.
$\approx 0.50$ μm, which is 500 nm: blue-green visible light. Our eyes evolved to see the light the Sun gives off most.

blocks.title: Earth's peak
blocks.q: Earth's average surface temperature is about 15 °C. At what wavelength does the ground glow brightest?
steps: Change to kelvins: $15 + 273 = 288$ K.
$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = 2898 \div 288 \approx 10.1$ μm.
That is infrared, about 20 times longer than the Sun's peak, because the Sun is about 20 times hotter in kelvins.

blocks.html: This split is what makes a greenhouse effect possible. Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb either kind of light. Water vapor, carbon dioxide and methane let most visible sunlight through but absorb strongly at many infrared wavelengths. So sunlight reaches the ground, while much of the ground's infrared is caught by the air above it. A gap called the atmospheric window, about 8 to 13 μm, lets some infrared escape straight to space; thermal cameras and weather satellites look through it.

Thinking only hot, glowing things give off light. Ice, clouds, the ground and your body all give off infrared radiation all the time; a thermal camera shows it. What changes with temperature is which wavelengths and how much. Check: any object above 0 K has a peak wavelength, $2898/T$ μm; a block of ice at 263 K peaks near 11 μm.

blocks.html: Wien's law (sunlight in, infrared out) tells you the color of an object's glow. This lesson answers the other question: how much energy does it give off? The answer climbs astonishingly fast with temperature.

Each square meter of a surface at temperature $T$ (in kelvins) gives off $$E = \sigma T^4, \qquad \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\,\text{K}^{-4}$$ This is the Stefan–Boltzmann law for a perfect emitter (a "blackbody"). Double the kelvin temperature and the energy goes up $2^4 = 16$ times.

Two effects multiply. A hotter surface sends out more light at every wavelength, and its peak moves to shorter wavelengths, where each bit of light carries more energy. Adding up the whole spectrum gives a fourth power. You can see it in a fire: embers that look only a little hotter than others glow far brighter. The ground, water and clouds are close to perfect emitters in the infrared, so $\sigma T^4$ describes them well.

blocks.title: Earth's glow
blocks.q: How much infrared does a square meter of ground at 15 °C give off?
steps: $E = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 6.88 \times 10^{9} \approx 390$ W/m²: about as much as four bright 100-watt bulbs, from every square meter of ground, day and night.

blocks.title: Twice as hot
blocks.q: A hot plate at 600 K is compared with a cool plate at 300 K. How many times as much energy does each square meter of the hot plate give off?
steps: $2^4 = 16$. No need to compute either energy separately.

blocks.title: A warmer day
blocks.q: A sidewalk warms from 10 °C to 20 °C. By what factor does its infrared glow grow?
steps: Use kelvins: 283 K and 293 K. (Using Celsius would say "twice as hot", which is wrong.)
The glow grows about 15%, not 16 times.

blocks.html: Expecting doubling the temperature to double the glow. The energy goes as $T^4$, so doubling the kelvin temperature multiplies it by 16, and tripling it by 81. A second trap is to double the Celsius temperature: 10 °C to 20 °C is only a 3.5% rise in kelvins. Check: always put kelvins into $T^4$.

blocks.name: es-energy
blocks.cap: The glow of a surface at 288 K and at 330 K. A rise of only 42 K (about 15%) makes the area under the curve, the total energy, about 72% bigger.

blocks.html: The fourth power is why Earth's temperature is so steady. If Earth warms a little, it gives off a lot more infrared, which pulls it back. A 1% rise in kelvin temperature raises the glow by about 4%. This is the strongest of all climate feedbacks, and it is a stabilizing one.

blocks.html: You know from why we have seasons that summer sunlight is stronger because the Sun climbs higher. This lesson shows exactly how much stronger, using sine and the height of the Sun above the horizon. Insolation is the sunlight energy arriving on each square meter of level ground.

A beam of sunlight that strikes the ground at a Sun height $h$ spreads over $1/\sin h$ times as much ground as when the Sun is overhead. So the energy on each square meter of level ground is $$E = E_{\text{beam}} \times \sin h$$ At noon, $h = 90^\circ - |\text{latitude} - \text{Sun's latitude}|$, where the Sun is overhead at 23.4° N on the June solstice, at the equator on the equinoxes and at 23.4° S on the December solstice.

Hold a flashlight straight down over a table: it makes a small, bright circle. Tilt it and the same light spreads into a long, dim oval. The beam carries the same energy either way, but tilted it shares that energy among more square centimeters. With the Sun at height $h$, a beam 1 m wide lands on a strip $1/\sin h$ meters long, so each square meter gets $\sin h$ of the overhead amount. At 30°, $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$: half.

blocks.name: es-earth-sun
blocks.cap: A beam of sunlight at a 30° Sun height spreads over twice the ground it would cover from straight overhead. Drag to change the angle and watch the energy per square meter.

blocks.title: A low winter Sun
blocks.q: At noon the Sun is 30° above the horizon, and the direct beam carries 1000 W for each square meter facing the Sun. How much falls on each square meter of level ground?
steps: The spreading factor is $\sin h = \sin 30^\circ = 0.5$.

blocks.title: Summer and winter at 40° N
blocks.q: Compare noon sunlight on level ground at 40° N on the June and December solstices, for the same beam.
steps: June: the Sun is overhead at 23.4° N, so $h = 90^\circ - (40^\circ - 23.4^\circ) = 73.4^\circ$.
December: the Sun is overhead at 23.4° S, so $h = 90^\circ - (40^\circ + 23.4^\circ) = 26.6^\circ$.
Ratio: $\sin 73.4^\circ / \sin 26.6^\circ \approx 0.958/0.448 \approx 2.1$.
Each square meter gets about twice the energy at noon in June, and the June day is also much longer.
blocks.a: About 2.1 times as much in June

blocks.html: Thinking low sunlight is weak mainly because it passes through more air. A low beam does cross more air, and haze and clouds take a bit more of it, but on a clear day the main effect is geometry: the beam spreads over more ground. Check: at a 30° Sun height the spreading alone cuts each square meter's share in half.

This is the engine of all weather. Near the equator the noon Sun is always high and insolation is large all year. Toward the poles the Sun stays low (and in winter does not rise at all), so far less energy lands on each square meter. That uneven heating drives the winds, the ocean currents and the storms of the rest of this course.

The day's length matters too. On the June solstice the North Pole gets 24 hours of sunlight, so even with a low Sun its total daily insolation tops that of the equator for a few weeks. Over a whole year, the equator still gets far more.

blocks.html: Not all the sunlight that lands on the ground stays there. Some bounces back to the sky. How much depends on the surface, and it changes the climate a great deal. This lesson uses percents of a number to follow the sunlight.

Albedo is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects: $$\text{albedo} = \frac{\text{reflected}}{\text{incoming}}$$ The rest is absorbed: absorbed = (1 − albedo) × incoming. Fresh snow has an albedo of about 0.8 to 0.9; the open ocean about 0.06; Earth as a whole about 0.30.

Light that hits a surface is either reflected or absorbed (sunlight does not pass through the ground). So the two shares must add to 100%. A white surface reflects most colors of light; a dark one absorbs them, and absorbed light becomes thermal energy. That is why a black car seat burns in summer and a white one stays cooler: same sunlight, different albedo.

blocks.title: Snow and ocean
blocks.q: Sunlight of 600 W/m² falls on fresh snow (albedo 0.85) and on open ocean (albedo 0.06). How much does each absorb?
steps: Snow absorbs $1 - 0.85 = 0.15$ of the light: $0.15 \times 600 = 90$ W/m².
Ocean absorbs $1 - 0.06 = 0.94$: $0.94 \times 600 = 564$ W/m².
The ocean absorbs more than six times as much as the snow under the same Sun.

blocks.title: Finding an albedo
blocks.q: A satellite measures 340 W/m² of sunlight arriving at a region and 102 W/m² reflected back. What is the albedo?
steps: Albedo = reflected ÷ incoming = $102 \div 340 = 0.30$.
So 30% is reflected and 70% absorbed: the same as Earth's average.

blocks.html: Reading a high albedo as "soaks up a lot of sunlight." Albedo measures what is reflected, so a high albedo means the surface absorbs less. Check: snow, with the highest albedo, stays cold in bright sunshine; dark asphalt, with one of the lowest, gets hot.

blocks.name: es-energy
blocks.cap: Earth's energy budget. Change the albedo: a whiter Earth reflects more sunlight and settles at a colder temperature; a darker Earth absorbs more and warms.

blocks.html: Albedo can change itself. When snow or sea ice melts, the dark ground or ocean underneath absorbs far more sunlight, which warms the area and melts more ice. This ice–albedo feedback is one reason the Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the planet.

blocks.html: You now have the pieces: sunlight arrives, albedo decides how much is absorbed, and every surface glows by the Stefan–Boltzmann law. Put them together and you can predict the temperature of a planet from two numbers, using a fourth root.

Earth warms until the infrared it sends to space equals the sunlight it absorbs: $$\sigma T_e^4 = \frac{S(1 - \alpha)}{4}$$ With $S = 1361$ W/m² (sunlight at Earth's distance) and albedo $\alpha = 0.30$, this gives $T_e \approx 255$ K, about −18 °C.

If Earth absorbed more than it gave off, it would warm; warming raises its glow as $T^4$, until the two match. That matching temperature is the balance. The factor of 4 comes from geometry: Earth intercepts sunlight on a disk of area $\pi R^2$ (its shadow), but it glows from its whole sphere, area $4\pi R^2$. Spread the sunlight over the sphere and each square meter gets, on average, $1361 \div 4 \approx 340$ W/m².

blocks.name: es-energy
blocks.cap: Sunlight in, reflected sunlight and infrared out. Change the albedo or the sunlight and watch the balance temperature move.

blocks.title: Earth with no greenhouse effect
blocks.q: Find Earth's balance temperature for $S = 1361$ W/m² and albedo 0.30.
steps: Average sunlight per square meter: $1361 \div 4 \approx 340$ W/m².
Absorbed: $(1 - 0.30) \times 340 \approx 238$ W/m².

blocks.title: A planet four times as far
blocks.q: A planet like Earth (same albedo) orbits four times as far from the Sun. What is its balance temperature?
steps: Sunlight spreads as the square of distance, so $S$ is $4^2 = 16$ times smaller.
$T_e$ goes as $S^{1/4}$, so it changes by $(1/16)^{1/4} = 1/2$.
$T_e \approx 255 \div 2 \approx 127$ K. No calculator needed.

blocks.title: A snowball Earth
blocks.q: If ice covered the planet and raised the albedo to 0.60, what would the balance temperature be?
steps: Absorbed: $(1 - 0.60) \times 340 = 136$ W/m².
A whiter planet absorbs less sunlight and settles much colder.

blocks.html: Forgetting to divide the sunlight by 4. Using the full 1361 W/m² would give about 360 K, near the boiling point of water. Earth catches sunlight on a disk but glows from a sphere four times the disk's area. Check: the average sunlight per square meter of Earth is about 340 W/m².

Earth's real average surface temperature is about 15 °C (288 K), some 33 °C warmer than this balance temperature. The difference is the greenhouse effect, the subject of the next lesson. Satellites confirm the outgoing side: Earth sends about 240 W/m² of infrared to space, just as this calculation predicts.

blocks.html: The energy balance predicts −18 °C for an Earth with no greenhouse gases, yet the real average is about 15 °C. Here is the simplest model that explains the difference: one layer of air that absorbs infrared.

An air layer that absorbs a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the ground's infrared glows both up and down. The ground must warm until the energy leaving to space again equals the sunlight absorbed: $$T_s = T_e\left(\frac{2}{2 - \varepsilon}\right)^{1/4}$$ With $\varepsilon = 0.78$ and $T_e = 255$ K, $T_s \approx 288$ K (15 °C).

Take a layer that absorbs all the ground's infrared ($\varepsilon = 1$). Seen from space, only the layer glows, so it must glow $\sigma T_e^4$ upward (about 240 W/m²). A layer glows equally from its top and bottom, so it also sends 240 W/m² down. Now the ground receives 240 W/m² of absorbed sunlight plus 240 W/m² from the layer, 480 W/m² in all, and must glow that much: $\sigma T_s^4 = 2\sigma T_e^4$, so $T_s = 2^{1/4}T_e \approx 1.19 \times 255 \approx 303$ K. A layer that absorbs only part of the infrared gives the formula in the key idea.

blocks.name: es-energy
blocks.cap: One air layer between the ground and space. Change how much infrared it absorbs (ε) and watch the ground's temperature: more absorbing gas, a warmer ground, with the same energy leaving to space.

blocks.title: A perfectly absorbing layer
blocks.q: If the air absorbed all of the ground's infrared and $T_e = 255$ K, what would the surface temperature be?
steps: With $\varepsilon = 1$: $T_s = 255 \times 2^{1/4}$.
$2^{1/4} \approx 1.189$, so $T_s \approx 303$ K, about 30 °C.
Too warm: the real air lets some infrared through the atmospheric window.

blocks.title: A partly absorbing layer
blocks.q: With $T_e = 255$ K and $\varepsilon = 0.78$, find $T_s$.
steps: $T_s \approx 255 \times 1.132 \approx 289$ K, close to the real 288 K.

blocks.html: Thinking greenhouse gases stop heat from leaving at all. In the model, Earth still sends exactly as much energy to space as it absorbs from the Sun, about 240 W/m². What changes is where it leaves from: more of it comes from the air layer, high and cold, instead of the warm ground. In the real atmosphere the infrared that escapes comes, on average, from about 5 km up, where the air is near −18 °C. To push out 240 W/m² from up there, the ground below must be warmer. Check: energy out to space = energy absorbed, before and after.

Adding more carbon dioxide raises $\varepsilon$ a little and lifts the average height from which infrared escapes. For a while Earth sends out less than it absorbs, and it warms until the balance returns at a higher surface temperature. The model leaves out a lot (convection, clouds, the sunlight the air absorbs), but this core idea survives in every full climate model.
The greenhouse effect is not the ozone hole. Ozone loss lets in more ultraviolet light; it is a different problem with a different cause.

blocks.html: Chemistry's specific heat explains one of the biggest patterns in climate: why a coastal town has mild summers and winters while a town far inland, at the same latitude, swings from hot to cold. The rule is $Q = mc\Delta T$.

Water takes about five times as much energy as dry sand to warm by one degree: $c_{\text{water}} = 4186$ J/(kg·°C), $c_{\text{sand}} \approx 830$ J/(kg·°C). With $$Q = mc\Delta T \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta T = \frac{Q}{mc}$$ the same energy changes water's temperature far less, so oceans warm and cool slowly and keep coasts mild.

Specific heat measures how much energy each kilogram stores per degree. Water molecules are held together by strong hydrogen bonds, and much of the energy you add goes into jiggling and stretching those bonds instead of raising the temperature. Two more things help the ocean: sunlight shines several meters into clear water, and waves and currents mix the heat down through tens of meters. On land, sunlight heats only the top few centimeters of soil, which cannot pass the heat down quickly. A thin, low-specific-heat layer heats and cools fast; a deep, high-specific-heat layer barely changes.

blocks.title: Same energy, different warming
blocks.q: A square meter of beach receives 41,860 J of sunlight energy into the top 1 kg of material. How much does 1 kg of water warm? How much would 1 kg of dry sand warm?
steps: Water: $\Delta T = Q/(mc) = 41{,}860 \div (1 \times 4186) = 10$ °C.
Sand: $\Delta T = 41{,}860 \div (1 \times 830) \approx 50$ °C.
Same energy, five times the warming in the sand. That is why sand burns your feet while the sea feels cool.

blocks.title: Energy to warm a lake layer
blocks.q: How much energy does it take to warm 1,000 kg of lake water (one cubic meter) by 2 °C?
steps: $Q = mc\Delta T = 1000 \times 4186 \times 2$.
$Q = 8{,}372{,}000$ J, about $8.4 \times 10^6$ J. A cubic meter of dry sand (about 1,600 kg) would need only about $2.7 \times 10^6$ J.

blocks.html: Thinking water warms slowly because it is wet or because it reflects sunlight. The open ocean has a very low albedo, so it absorbs most of the sunlight that hits it. It warms slowly because each kilogram needs much more energy per degree ($Q = mc\Delta T$), and because mixing spreads that energy through a deep layer. Check: compare the $c$ values, 4186 versus about 830.

blocks.cap: A sea breeze: by day the land heats faster than the sea, warm air rises over the land, and cooler sea air flows in to replace it. Switch to night and the pattern reverses.

blocks.html: Climate data show the effect. Seattle, on the Pacific side of North America, swings about 14 °C between its coldest and warmest months; Chicago, deep inside the continent at a similar latitude, swings about 28 °C (rounded NOAA 1991–2020 normals). Try it in the Zeroth Law lab: press a block of water against blocks of granite or iron and watch where their temperatures meet. Water barely moves.

blocks.html: In changes of state you saw that melting and boiling take in energy without raising the temperature, and freezing and condensing give it back. In the atmosphere this hidden energy, carried in water vapor, is one of the biggest energy flows on the planet. It builds clouds and powers storms. It follows the warming of water you met in why coasts stay mild, but it is far larger.

Evaporating water takes in its latent heat of vaporization, about $L_v = 2.5 \times 10^6$ J/kg near 0 °C ($2.26 \times 10^6$ J/kg at 100 °C), and condensing vapor releases the same amount: $$Q = mL$$ Melting ice takes in $L_f = 3.34 \times 10^5$ J/kg, and freezing gives it back.

In liquid water, molecules cling to each other with hydrogen bonds. To escape as vapor, a molecule must break free, and that takes energy, which comes from the surroundings and cools them. That is why sweating cools you and a wet towel feels cold. The energy is not lost: it rides along in the vapor. When the vapor condenses into cloud droplets, the bonds form again and the energy is released into the air around the droplets, warming it.

blocks.title: How big is latent heat?
blocks.q: Compare the energy to evaporate 1 kg of water with the energy to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C.
steps: Evaporating: $Q = mL_v = 1 \times 2.5 \times 10^6 = 2{,}500{,}000$ J.
Warming by 1 °C: $Q = mc\Delta T = 1 \times 4186 \times 1 = 4186$ J.
Ratio: $2{,}500{,}000 \div 4186 \approx 600$. Evaporating a kilogram of water takes as much energy as warming it by about 600 degrees, if it could stay liquid.

blocks.title: Warming a cloud
blocks.q: In a rising cloud, 2 g of water vapor condenses in each kilogram of air. How much energy is released, and by about how much could it warm that kilogram of air? (For air, $c_p = 1005$ J/(kg·°C).)
steps: Energy: $Q = mL_v = 0.002 \times 2.5 \times 10^6 = 5000$ J.
Warming: $\Delta T = Q/(mc_p) = 5000 \div (1 \times 1005) \approx 5$ °C.
That is why saturated rising air cools more slowly than dry air.

blocks.html: Thinking condensation cools the air because it happens in cool air. Condensation happens when air cools to its dew point, but the condensing itself releases heat into the air. Evaporation cools; condensation warms. Check: a puddle drying takes energy from the ground (cooling); a cloud forming gives energy to the air (warming).

blocks.cap: A parcel of moist air rising. Below the cloud base it cools at the dry rate; inside the cloud, condensation releases latent heat and it cools more slowly, so it stays warmer than the air around it and keeps rising.

blocks.html: Latent heat moves enormous amounts of energy around Earth. Averaged over the globe, evaporation is the biggest way the surface sends energy up into the air, roughly a quarter of all the sunlight arriving at the top of the atmosphere (NASA). The energy travels as vapor, sometimes thousands of kilometers, and comes out where clouds form. A hurricane is a machine that runs on it: warm ocean water evaporates, and the vapor condenses in the storm's towering clouds.

blocks.html: In the water cycle, water evaporates, travels as invisible vapor and condenses into clouds. This unit measures that vapor. Meteorologists count it by the pressure the vapor molecules add to the air, the vapor pressure $e$, in hectopascals. Temperatures here are in Celsius (see temperature scales).

Air is saturated when water evaporates and condenses at the same rate, so the amount of vapor stops changing. The vapor pressure at saturation, $e_s$, depends only on the temperature, and it climbs steeply: it roughly doubles for every 10 °C of warming (about 6 to 7% per degree).

Picture the surface of a puddle. Water molecules jiggle, and the fastest ones break free into the air: evaporation. Meanwhile vapor molecules flying around hit the surface and stick: condensation. Evaporation depends on how warm the water is; condensation depends on how many vapor molecules there are. When the two rates match, the vapor stops increasing: saturation. Notice what is missing: the nitrogen and oxygen of the air play no part. A sealed jar of water with all the air pumped out reaches the same saturation vapor pressure. Warmer water sends molecules off faster, so it takes more vapor to balance them.

blocks.title: Room for more vapor?
blocks.q: Air at 20 °C has a vapor pressure of 15.0 hPa. Is it saturated? How much more vapor pressure could it reach?
steps: From the table, saturation at 20 °C is 23.4 hPa.
15.0 hPa is below that, so the air is not saturated; more water can evaporate into it.
It could gain $23.4 - 15.0 = 8.4$ hPa before evaporation and condensation balance.

blocks.title: Cooling past saturation
blocks.q: Air at 25 °C has a vapor pressure of 23.4 hPa. Overnight it cools to 15 °C. What happens to the vapor?
steps: At 20 °C the saturation pressure is 23.4 hPa, so the air becomes saturated when it cools to 20 °C.
At 15 °C saturation is only 17.0 hPa, so the vapor pressure can't stay at 23.4.
About $23.4 - 17.0 = 6.4$ hPa worth of vapor condenses into dew or fog.

blocks.html: Picturing air as a sponge that "holds" water, with warm air holding more. Saturation depends on the temperature of the water and vapor, not on the air; it would happen with no air at all. Saying "warm air can hold more water" gives the right numbers, but the cause is the temperature, not the air. Check: in a vacuum jar at 20 °C, water still evaporates until the vapor pressure reaches 23.4 hPa.

Another way to count vapor is the mass of vapor in each kilogram of air. At sea level, saturated air holds about 3.8 g/kg at 0 °C, 7.6 g/kg at 10 °C, 14.7 g/kg at 20 °C and 27 g/kg at 30 °C: the same steep climb.

blocks.html: The forecast says the humidity is 90%. Ninety percent of what? Relative humidity compares the vapor in the air with the saturation amount at the air's current temperature. Because saturation depends so strongly on temperature, relative humidity can change all day while the amount of vapor stays the same.
$$\text{RH} = \frac{e}{e_s(T)} \times 100\%$$ where $e$ is the vapor pressure and $e_s(T)$ is the saturation vapor pressure at the air temperature $T$. At 100% the air is saturated.

The top of the fraction is the vapor that is really there. The bottom is the saturation amount, which grows fast when the air warms. Warm the air and the bottom grows, so RH falls, even though not one molecule of vapor left. Cool the air and RH rises. That is why RH is usually highest around dawn, the coolest time of day, and lowest in mid-afternoon.

blocks.q: A cold morning: 5 °C and 100% RH. A desert afternoon: 35 °C and 20% RH. Which air holds more water vapor?
steps: Cold morning: $e = 1.00 \times 8.7 = 8.7$ hPa.

The "dry" desert air has about 30% more vapor than the "saturated" morning air.

blocks.title: Same air, warmer
blocks.q: Saturated air at 10 °C (RH 100%) warms to 25 °C without gaining or losing vapor. What is its new RH?
steps: The vapor stays at $e = 12.3$ hPa (saturation at 10 °C).
At 25 °C, $e_s = 31.7$ hPa, so RH = $12.3 \div 31.7 \approx 39\%$.

blocks.html: Reading high relative humidity as "lots of water vapor." RH is a ratio, and its bottom changes with temperature. A cold morning at 100% can have less vapor than a hot desert afternoon at 20%. Check: multiply RH by $e_s$ at each temperature before comparing two places or times.

blocks.html: Relative humidity (RH) shifts whenever the temperature changes. Forecasters prefer a number that stays put when the air warms or cools: the dew point. It measures the vapor itself, in degrees.

The dew point $T_d$ is the temperature the air must cool to, with its vapor unchanged, to become saturated: $e_s(T_d) = e$. A higher dew point means more water vapor. The dew point can never be above the air temperature, and the spread $T - T_d$ tells how close the air is to saturation.

Cool air without adding or removing vapor and $e$ stays the same, while the saturation pressure $e_s$ falls. At some temperature they meet; that is the dew point. Since $e_s$ depends only on temperature, knowing $T_d$ tells you $e$ exactly: the dew point is the vapor pressure written as a temperature. That is why it does not change from dawn to afternoon unless vapor is added or removed.

blocks.title: Will there be fog?
blocks.q: At sunset the temperature is 18 °C and the dew point is 9 °C. The forecast low is 8 °C, on a clear, calm night. What should you expect by morning?
steps: The air will cool below its dew point (8 °C is below 9 °C).
Once it reaches 9 °C it is saturated; further cooling condenses vapor.
Expect dew on the grass and likely patches of fog. If the dew point were below 0 °C, frost would form instead.

blocks.html: Using relative humidity to judge how muggy it feels. Sticky, muggy air is about how much vapor there is, which slows the evaporation of sweat. A winter morning at 100% RH (dew point 2 °C) feels crisp, while a summer afternoon at 32 °C and 50% RH (dew point about 20 °C) feels muggy. Check the dew point instead: the National Weather Service describes dew points below about 55 °F (13 °C) as dry and comfortable, 55 to 65 °F (13 to 18 °C) as sticky, and above 65 °F as oppressive.

blocks.html: Dew, frost and fog. On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat by infrared to the sky and cools fastest. When it reaches the dew point, dew forms on grass and cars. If the dew point is below 0 °C, vapor turns straight to ice: frost (the dew point is then called the frost point). When a layer of air near the ground cools to its dew point, droplets form in the air itself: fog. Fog is a cloud at ground level.

blocks.html: Almost every cloud forms in air that is rising. The reason is simple to state and surprising to explain: rising air cools. You know that pressure falls with height; this lesson shows why that makes a rising bubble of air colder, even though nothing outside cools it.

A parcel (a bubble) of rising air moves into lower pressure, expands, and cools by about 9.8 °C for every kilometer it rises, as long as no water condenses in it. This is the dry adiabatic lapse rate ("adiabatic" means no heat flows in or out). Sinking air is squeezed and warms at the same rate.

As the parcel rises, the air around it presses less, so the parcel spreads out, pushing the surrounding air aside. Pushing is work, and the energy for it comes from the parcel's own molecules, which slow down: the parcel cools. Air is a poor conductor and the parcel moves fast, so almost no heat flows in to make up the loss. The rate comes from energy bookkeeping: for each kilogram, the drop in thermal energy $c_p\,\Delta T$ matches the gain in height energy $g\,\Delta z$, so $\Delta T/\Delta z = -g/c_p = -9.8 \div 1005 \approx -0.0098$ °C per meter, or 9.8 °C per km.

In the Science Lab's First Law lab, the first law is written $\Delta U = Q - W$, where $W$ is the work done by the gas. For a rising parcel, $Q \approx 0$ (no heat in or out) and $W > 0$ (it expands and pushes), so $\Delta U < 0$: its internal energy and temperature drop. Physics 2 and chemistry write the same law as $\Delta U = Q + W$ with $W$ the work done on the gas; there $W$ is negative for an expanding parcel, and the result is the same. Try it in the lab: let the gas expand with no heat added and watch it cool.

blocks.title: Lifting a parcel
blocks.q: A parcel of dry air at 25 °C rises 2 km without reaching saturation. What is its temperature?
steps: It cools 9.8 °C for each km: $2 \times 9.8 = 19.6$ °C.

blocks.title: Sinking air
blocks.q: Air at 3 km has a temperature of −5 °C. It sinks to the ground (0 km) without any condensation or evaporation. What is its temperature when it arrives?
steps: Sinking air is squeezed and warms 9.8 °C per km: $3 \times 9.8 = 29.4$ °C.
$-5 + 29.4 = 24.4$ °C. Sinking air arrives warm and dry, which is why sinking air clears the sky.

blocks.html: Thinking rising air cools because it gets closer to cold space or farther from the warm ground. A parcel cools because it expands, doing work on the air around it; no heat has to leave it. Check: sinking air warms by the same rate even when it comes down into a cold valley, because it is being squeezed.
Many problems round the dry rate to 10 °C per km to make the arithmetic easy; they say so when they do.

blocks.html: Since rising air cools, clouds form wherever air is lifted far enough to cool to its dew point. So the question "where will clouds form?" becomes "what lifts the air?" There are four main answers.

Air is lifted by convection (the ground heats a bubble of air, which rises), by mountains (wind forces air up a slope: orographic lifting), at fronts (a wedge of dense cold air pushes under warmer air) and by convergence (winds crowd together near the ground, and the air has nowhere to go but up).

Each one gives air a reason to go up. In convection, a patch of sunny ground heats the air above it, and the warmer, less dense bubble floats upward, like the warm air in a hot-air balloon. Over mountains the wind has to go somewhere, and the slope forces it up. At a front, the denser cold air stays low and slides under the warm air, lifting it. Where winds flow together, as when sea breezes from two coasts meet over Florida on summer afternoons, air piles up and is squeezed upward.

items: Convection: puffy cumulus over sunny fields on summer afternoons; thunderstorms when it is strong.
Orographic lifting: clouds and rain on the windward slopes of mountains.
Frontal lifting: bands of cloud and rain along cold and warm fronts.
Convergence: lines of storms where winds meet, and the rising air at the center of low-pressure systems.

steps: There is no wind to push air up a slope, and no front is mentioned.
The dark field heats in the sun much faster than the lake, warming the air above it.
Warm bubbles rise from the field: convection.

blocks.html: Thinking clouds are fed by water evaporating straight up into them, like steam rising off a pot. Vapor is in the air everywhere, mostly invisible; clouds form only where air is lifted and cools to its dew point. Check: a cloud base is flat and level across the sky. That flat base is the height where rising air reaches its dew point, the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.html: A rising parcel cools at the dry rate until it reaches its dew point. Then vapor condenses and a cloud begins. That height is the cloud base, and you can predict it from a thermometer and a dew-point reading at the ground.

As a parcel rises, its temperature falls about 10 °C per km and its dew point falls about 2 °C per km, so the gap between them closes about 8 °C per km. The cloud base is about $$h \approx 125\ \text{m} \times (T - T_d)$$ with $T - T_d$ in °C (about 228 ft per °F of spread).

Why does the dew point fall at all? The parcel keeps its vapor, but as it expands, the vapor is spread through more volume, so the vapor pressure drops along with the total pressure. Lower vapor pressure means a lower dew point: about 1.8 to 2 °C per km. Meanwhile the temperature drops about 9.8 °C per km. So the two close in at about $9.8 - 1.8 = 8$ °C per km, and each degree of spread takes about $1000 \div 8 = 125$ m to close.

blocks.q: At the ground the temperature is 30 °C and the dew point is 22 °C. About how high is the base of the cumulus clouds?
steps: Height: $8 \times 125 = 1000$ m.
Check: rising 1 km, the parcel cools to about $30 - 10 = 20$ °C, and its dew point drops to $22 - 2 = 20$ °C. They meet.

blocks.q: A pilot reads 75 °F with a dew point of 53 °F. About how high is the cloud base, in feet?
steps: Height: $22 \times 228 \approx 5000$ ft.
Pilots often use the same rule as "spread in °F ÷ 4.4, in thousands of feet": $22 \div 4.4 = 5$ thousand feet.

blocks.q: Cumulus bases are at 1500 m on an afternoon when the temperature is 27 °C. Estimate the dew point.

blocks.html: Keeping the rising parcel's dew point fixed. That makes the gap close at 10 °C per km, giving 100 m per degree, and puts the cloud base too low. The dew point also drops about 2 °C per km, so the gap closes at about 8 °C per km: 125 m per degree. Check: at the cloud base, the parcel's temperature and dew point should both have dropped, and be equal.

This is why fair-weather cumulus all have flat bases at the same height: every bubble from the same ground air reaches its dew point at the same level. When the spread is near zero, the "cloud base" is at the ground: fog.

blocks.html: Above the cloud base, a rising parcel is saturated, and every bit more cooling condenses some vapor. Condensing releases latent heat inside the parcel. That changes how fast it cools.

A saturated parcel cools more slowly than a dry one: about 6 °C per km on average (the moist adiabatic lapse rate). It is about 4 °C per km in warm, humid air near the ground and approaches the dry rate (9.8 °C per km) in very cold air high up. Problems here use 6 °C per km unless they say otherwise.

Expansion still cools the parcel by 9.8 °C for each km. But as it cools, vapor condenses, and each gram of vapor that condenses gives about 2500 J back to the parcel's air. That pays back part of the cooling. Warm saturated air condenses a lot of vapor for each degree of cooling (saturation climbs so steeply with temperature), so it gets a big payback and cools only about 4 °C per km. Cold air has little vapor left to condense, so it cools almost as fast as dry air.

blocks.title: Climbing inside a cloud
blocks.q: A parcel is saturated at its cloud base, 1 km up, at 16 °C. It keeps rising to 5 km. What is its temperature? (Use 6 °C per km.)
steps: It climbs $5 - 1 = 4$ km while saturated.
Cooling: $4 \times 6 = 24$ °C.
$16 - 24 = -8$ °C. A dry parcel would have cooled 40 °C, to −24 °C.

blocks.title: From the ground to the top of a cloud
blocks.q: Ground air at 26 °C with a dew point of 18 °C is lifted to 4 km. Use 10 °C per km (dry), 2 °C per km for the dew point and 6 °C per km (moist). Find its temperature at 4 km.
steps: Cloud base: the spread of 8 °C closes at 8 °C per km, so the base is at 1 km.
At the base: $26 - 10 \times 1 = 16$ °C (and the dew point is $18 - 2 = 16$ °C).
From 1 km to 4 km, moist: $16 - 6 \times 3 = -2$ °C.

blocks.html: Thinking the released latent heat warms a rising cloud parcel. The parcel still cools as it rises; the latent heat only slows the cooling, from 9.8 to about 6 °C per km. Check: in any moist-ascent answer, the parcel's temperature at the top must be lower than at the cloud base.

blocks.html: Put the lifting of air by a mountain together with the moist rate and you get one of the clearest patterns on any climate map: a wet side and a dry side of every big mountain range, and warm, dry winds pouring down the lee slope.

Air forced up a mountain cools at the dry rate to its cloud base, then at the slower moist rate while it rains out its moisture. Coming down the far side it is no longer saturated, so it warms at the dry rate the whole way. It arrives warmer and drier than it started: a rain shadow and a warm downslope wind (a foehn, or in the Rocky Mountains a chinook).

The trip down is not the trip up in reverse. On the way up, part of the climb happens at the moist rate (about 6 °C per km), so the air loses less temperature than it would have dry. On the way down there are no droplets left to evaporate, so it gains temperature at the full dry rate (about 10 °C per km). The extra warmth is the latent heat released when its vapor condensed and fell as rain on the windward side. The water left; the heat stayed in the air.

steps: Cloud base: spread 8 °C, closing at 8 °C per km: 1 km up, at $20 - 10 = 10$ °C.
From 1 km to the 3 km peak, moist: $10 - 6 \times 2 = -2$ °C at the top.
Down 3 km, dry: $-2 + 10 \times 3 = 28$ °C.
It ends 8 °C warmer than it started.

blocks.title: How dry is it?
blocks.q: In the example above, the air at the top is saturated at −2 °C, so its dew point is −2 °C. Coming down, its dew point rises about 2 °C per km. What are its dew point and relative humidity at the lee foot? ($e_s$ at 4 °C ≈ 8.1 hPa; at 28 °C ≈ 37.8 hPa.)
steps: Dew point at the foot: $-2 + 2 \times 3 = 4$ °C, down from 12 °C at the start.
RH = $e_s(T_d)/e_s(T) = 8.1 \div 37.8 \approx 0.21$, about 21%.
Warm and dry: grass and brush dry out fast in such winds.

blocks.title: No cloud, no warming
blocks.q: Air at 15 °C with a dew point of 0 °C crosses a 1 km ridge. Where does it end up?
steps: Its cloud base would be $15 \times 125 = 1875$ m, above the ridge, so no cloud forms.
It cools 10 °C going up and warms 10 °C coming down: it ends at 15 °C, just where it started.
Without condensation there is no rain shadow and no extra warmth.

blocks.html: Thinking a warm downslope wind blows in from somewhere warm. It is the same air that left the windward side; it warms by being squeezed as it sinks, and ends warmer than it started because it kept the latent heat released when its vapor rained out. Check: the extra warmth only appears if a cloud formed and rained on the way up.

blocks.html: A lifted parcel cools at the dry rate or the moist rate. Whether it keeps going up, building towering clouds, or sinks back, depends on the air around it. That is the question of stability.

Lift a parcel and compare it with the surrounding air at its new height. If the parcel is warmer, it is less dense and keeps rising: unstable. If it is colder, it sinks back: stable. Compare how fast the surroundings cool with height (the environmental lapse rate) with the parcel's rate: faster than 9.8 °C per km is absolutely unstable; slower than the moist rate (about 6) is absolutely stable; in between is conditionally unstable, stable for dry air but unstable once the parcel is saturated.

A parcel's fate is a race between two temperatures. The parcel cools at a fixed rate (dry or moist). The surrounding air has whatever temperature profile the weather has given it. If the surroundings get colder with height faster than the parcel does, the parcel finds itself warmer than its neighbors at every step up, and buoyancy pushes it higher: a runaway. If the surroundings cool more slowly, the parcel becomes the colder, denser one and sinks back. An inversion, where the air gets warmer with height, is the most stable of all.

blocks.name: es-parcel
blocks.cap: The black line is the surrounding air; drag its points to change how fast it cools. Red shading means the parcel is warmer than its surroundings (it rises on its own); blue means colder (it sinks back).

blocks.title: A lift test
blocks.q: The surrounding air is 20 °C at the ground and cools 8 °C per km. A dry (unsaturated) parcel is lifted from the ground to 1 km. Use 10 °C per km for the parcel. Is the air stable for it?
steps: Parcel at 1 km: $20 - 10 = 10$ °C.
Surroundings at 1 km: $20 - 8 = 12$ °C.
The parcel is 2 °C colder, so it is denser and sinks back: stable for dry air.

blocks.title: The same air, saturated
blocks.q: Now the parcel in the example is saturated from the start and cools at 6 °C per km. Is it stable?
steps: Parcel at 1 km: $20 - 6 = 14$ °C; surroundings: 12 °C.
The parcel is 2 °C warmer and keeps rising: unstable.
Since 8 °C per km lies between 6 and 10, this air is conditionally unstable: the condition is saturation.

blocks.html: Judging stability by the temperature at the ground. A hot day is not always unstable, and a cold one is not always stable. What matters is how fast the surrounding air cools with height compared with a rising parcel. Check: compute both temperatures at the same height above the ground and compare them.

items: Environment cools faster than 9.8 °C per km: absolutely unstable (common only right above hot ground).
Between about 6 and 9.8 °C per km: conditionally unstable (the average, 6.5 °C per km, is here).
Slower than about 6 °C per km: absolutely stable.
Warmer with height (an inversion): very stable; it traps haze and smog under it.

blocks.html: Clouds form where air is lifted and cools to its dew point, and their shapes record how the air was moving. Heaped clouds grow in rising bubbles of unstable air; flat sheets form where stable air is lifted gently over a wide area. A cloud's name tells you both its height and its shape.

Cloud names are built from a few Latin roots: cirro- (high, wispy, like a curl of hair), alto- (middle height), strato- (a flat layer), cumulo- (a heap) and nimbo- or -nimbus (bringing rain or snow). High clouds are about 5 to 13 km up, middle clouds about 2 to 7 km, and low clouds below about 2 km; cumulonimbus towers through all three.

Shape follows motion. A bubble of warm, unstable air rises on its own, so its cloud bulges upward in heaps (cumulus); if the bubble keeps rising past the freezing level and to the top of the troposphere, it becomes a cumulonimbus, a thunderstorm. Stable air lifted slowly over a large area, such as ahead of a warm front, cools evenly and makes a flat, wide sheet (stratus, altostratus). Height follows temperature: high clouds form where it is far below freezing, so they are made of ice crystals, which is why they look thin and wispy and can make halos around the Sun or Moon.

blocks.title: Name the cloud

steps: A ring (halo) is made by light bending through ice crystals, so the cloud is high.
A veil that covers the sky is a layer: strato-.

blocks.title: Rain or showers?
blocks.q: One afternoon brings brief, heavy downpours with thunder; another day brings light, steady rain from morning to night. Which cloud made each?
steps: Brief, heavy showers with thunder come from a tall heap that rose fast in unstable air: cumulonimbus.
Long, steady, gentle rain comes from a thick, wide layer: nimbostratus.

blocks.html: Thinking dark clouds are made of something different from white ones, such as smoke or dirt. Every cloud is made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. A thick or dense cloud scatters and absorbs most of the sunlight before it gets through, so its base looks dark from below; the same cloud seen from an airplane above is bright white. Check: the darkest clouds are usually the thickest ones, like nimbostratus and cumulonimbus.

blocks.html: A cloud is made of droplets so small that thousands would fit across a millimeter. Most clouds never rain. To fall as rain, droplets must grow enormously, and you can measure how much with the volume of a sphere. The type of cloud and its temperature decide which of two growth processes does it.

A typical cloud droplet has a radius of about 10 μm; a raindrop about 1 mm (1000 μm), 100 times wider. Volume grows as the cube of the radius, so one raindrop holds about $100^3 = 1{,}000{,}000$ cloud droplets. Drops grow by collision and coalescence (bigger drops fall faster, hit smaller ones and join them) or by the ice-crystal process (in clouds colder than 0 °C, ice crystals grow while the water droplets around them evaporate).

A droplet 10 μm in radius falls only about a centimeter per second through still air, so even a gentle updraft holds it up, and it would evaporate long before it fell out of the cloud. A 2 mm raindrop falls about 6.5 m/s. So size is everything. In a cold cloud, vapor condenses onto ice more readily than onto water: at −10 °C, saturation over ice is about 10% lower than over water. Air that is just saturated for the water droplets is supersaturated for the ice crystals, so the crystals grow fast and the droplets shrink. The crystals become snowflakes heavy enough to fall, and many melt into rain on the way down. Much of the rain in the middle latitudes starts as snow high in the cloud.

blocks.title: How many droplets?
blocks.q: How many cloud droplets of radius 10 μm make one raindrop of radius 1 mm?
steps: Same units: 1 mm = 1000 μm.
Ratio of radii: $1000 \div 10 = 100$.
Volume goes as the cube: $100^3 = 1{,}000{,}000$ droplets.

blocks.title: A drizzle drop
blocks.q: A drizzle drop has a radius of 0.1 mm. How many 10 μm droplets does it hold?
steps: $10^3 = 1000$ droplets: a drizzle drop is still a thousand times smaller in volume than a raindrop.

blocks.title: Too slow to fall
blocks.q: A droplet falls about 1.2 cm/s. How long would it take to fall 1 km?
steps: Time: $100{,}000 \div 1.2 \approx 83{,}000$ s, about 23 hours. It would evaporate in the drier air below the cloud long before.

blocks.html: Thinking cloud droplets simply get heavy and fall. A droplet is so small that the slightest updraft holds it up, and in the dry air below the cloud it would evaporate in seconds to minutes. It must grow about 100 times wider, a million times in volume, before it can fall out as rain. Check: (R ÷ r)³ should come out near a million for real raindrops.

blocks.html: Most winter precipitation starts as snow high in the cloud (see how raindrops grow). What reaches the ground depends on the temperatures the falling snowflake meets on the way down. Forecasters read these layers from weather-balloon soundings.

If the air is below freezing all the way down: snow. If a warm layer (above 0 °C) melts the flakes and the air stays warm to the ground: rain. If the melted drops then fall through a deep cold layer, they refreeze into ice pellets: sleet. If the cold layer near the ground is too shallow to refreeze them, they land as liquid and freeze on contact with cold surfaces: freezing rain.

Melting and freezing take time and energy. A flake has to fall through enough warm air, for long enough, to melt completely; a thin or barely warm layer leaves it partly melted. A melted drop has to fall through enough cold air to give up its latent heat and freeze; a thin cold layer lets it reach the ground still liquid but colder than 0 °C ("supercooled"). Supercooled drops freeze the instant they touch a cold road, branch or power line, coating it in a glaze of ice.

blocks.title: Read the sounding
blocks.q: Snow forms at 3 km. Below it, the air is above freezing (up to +4 °C) from 2.4 km down to 1.2 km, then below freezing from 1.2 km to the ground, reaching −8 °C at the ground. What falls?
steps: The thick warm layer melts the snowflakes into raindrops.
The cold layer below is deep (1.2 km) and cold, so the drops refreeze before landing.
Ice pellets: sleet.

blocks.title: A thin cold layer
blocks.q: Same warm layer aloft, but now the air is above freezing down to 200 m, with only −2 °C at the ground. What falls?
steps: The warm layer melts the snow.
The cold layer is only 200 m deep and barely below freezing: the drops stay liquid.
They freeze on contact with the cold ground: freezing rain.

blocks.html: Thinking sleet and freezing rain are the same. Sleet freezes in the air and lands as ice pellets that bounce; freezing rain lands as liquid and freezes on contact, building a smooth glaze on everything it touches. Check where the drops freeze: in the air (sleet) or on the ground (freezing rain). The difference comes from the depth of the cold layer near the ground.

blocks.html: You know from Earth Science that wind blows from high to low pressure. Here we measure that push. On a weather map, lines of equal pressure called isobars are drawn every 4 hPa. The pressure gradient is how fast the pressure changes across them: a rate of change with distance.

The pressure gradient force pushes air from high toward low pressure, straight across the isobars. Its size per kilogram of air is $$a = \frac{1}{\rho}\,\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta n}$$ where $\Delta p$ is the pressure difference (in Pa) across a distance $\Delta n$ (in m) and $\rho$ is the air's density. Where isobars are close together, the gradient and the push are strong, and winds are strong.

Picture a box of air with high pressure on its west face and lower pressure on its east face. The air on the west pushes harder than the air on the east, so the box feels a net push eastward, toward the low. Double the pressure difference, or halve the distance it is spread over, and the net push doubles. Dividing by the density turns force into acceleration: the same push moves thin air faster than dense air.

blocks.name: es-wind
blocks.cap: Isobars around a high and a low. The pressure gradient force (arrow) points straight across the isobars toward the low and is strongest where they crowd together. Change the spacing to see the push grow and shrink.

blocks.title: Reading the gradient
blocks.q: Two isobars, 1012 hPa and 1008 hPa, are 200 km apart. What is the pressure gradient in hPa per 100 km?
steps: Pressure difference: $1012 - 1008 = 4$ hPa.
Per 100 km: $4 \div 200 \times 100 = 2$ hPa per 100 km.

blocks.title: How hard is the push?
blocks.q: For that gradient, with air density 1.2 kg/m³, what acceleration does the pressure gradient give the air?
steps: $\Delta p = 4$ hPa = 400 Pa; $\Delta n = 200$ km = 200,000 m.
Small, but acting for an hour (3600 s) it would add about 6 m/s of speed if nothing pushed back.

blocks.html: Thinking wind blows straight from high to low pressure. The pressure gradient force does point straight across the isobars, and that is how air starts to move. But as soon as it moves, Earth's spin turns it (the next lesson), and above the ground it ends up blowing along the isobars. Check: on a weather map, upper-level winds follow the lines, and surface winds cross them only at a slant.

Pressure differences that drive the wind are small: a strong gradient is only a few hectopascals per 100 km, less than 1% of the total pressure. A hurricane's eye can be 50 to 100 hPa below its surroundings across a short distance, which is why its winds are so violent.

blocks.html: Air pushed by the pressure gradient force does not keep going straight on a map. In Earth Science you met the Coriolis effect turning the global winds; this lesson measures it, using the sine of the latitude.

On the spinning Earth, anything moving across the surface is turned to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The turning is measured by the Coriolis parameter $$f = 2\Omega\sin\varphi, \qquad \Omega = 7.29 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$$ where $\varphi$ is the latitude. The sideways acceleration is $f \times$ speed. It is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles, and it changes only the direction of the wind, never its speed.

Roll a ball straight across a spinning merry-go-round. Seen from the ground, the ball goes straight; but the merry-go-round turns underneath it, so to a rider the path curves. Earth is a slowly spinning platform. Looking down on the North Pole, Earth turns counterclockwise, and moving air seems to curve right; looking down on the South Pole it turns clockwise, and moving air curves left. How much the ground turns under you depends on latitude: at a pole the ground spins fully around once a day, at the equator it doesn't spin about the vertical at all. That is where the $\sin\varphi$ comes from.

blocks.name: es-wind
blocks.cap: A ball rolled across a spinning table really goes straight, but someone riding the table sees it curve. Switch the spin direction to see the Southern Hemisphere.

blocks.title: The Coriolis parameter at 45° N
blocks.q: Find $f$ at 45° latitude, and the sideways acceleration of a 10 m/s wind there.
steps: $\sin 45^\circ \approx 0.707$.
$f = 2 \times 7.29 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.707 \approx 1.03 \times 10^{-4}$ s⁻¹.
Acceleration: $f \times v = 1.03 \times 10^{-4} \times 10 \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m/s², turning the wind to the right.

blocks.title: Which way does it turn?
blocks.q: Air moves south (toward the equator) at 30° S. Which way does the Coriolis effect turn it?
steps: In the Southern Hemisphere, moving air is turned to its left.
Facing south, your left is east.
It is turned toward the east.

blocks.html: Thinking the Coriolis effect speeds the wind up, or that it is strongest at the equator. It always acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes direction only, and it grows with $\sin\varphi$: zero at the equator, largest at the poles. Hurricanes need it to spin up, which is why they almost never form within about 5° of the equator. Check: at 30° latitude, $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$, so $f$ is half its polar value.

The Coriolis effect matters for winds and ocean currents that travel hundreds of kilometers over hours or days. It is far too weak to decide which way water swirls down a sink or toilet; the shape of the basin and how the water was poured matter much more.

blocks.html: Air pushed toward low pressure is turned by the Coriolis effect. High above the ground, where nothing rubs against it, the turning goes on until the two forces balance. The result is one of the most useful facts in meteorology: upper-level winds blow along the isobars.

Aloft, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance, and the wind blows parallel to the isobars, with low pressure on its left in the Northern Hemisphere (on its right in the Southern). This geostrophic wind has speed $$V = \frac{1}{\rho f}\,\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta n}$$ so it is faster where the isobars are closer together.

Start a parcel at rest: the pressure gradient force pulls it toward the low. As it speeds up, the Coriolis force, at right angles to its motion and growing with its speed, bends it to the right (in the north). It keeps bending until it moves along the isobars; then the Coriolis force points straight back toward the high, exactly opposite the pressure gradient force. Balanced forces mean no more change: the wind blows steadily along the lines. Setting the two equal, $\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta n} = fV$, gives the formula. The density comes from the gas law, and thinner air aloft blows faster for the same gradient.

blocks.name: es-wind
blocks.cap: A parcel released from rest aloft: pushed toward the low, turned by the Coriolis force, it swings around until it runs along the isobars with the low on its left.

blocks.title: Speed of the wind aloft
blocks.q: At 45° N ($f = 1.03 \times 10^{-4}$ s⁻¹), the pressure changes by 4 hPa over 200 km, and the air density is 1.2 kg/m³. Find the geostrophic wind.
steps: $\Delta p = 400$ Pa, $\Delta n = 200{,}000$ m, so $\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta n} = 0.002$ Pa/m.
$V = \dfrac{0.002}{1.2 \times 1.03 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 16$ m/s.
At 5.5 km, where the density is about 0.7 kg/m³, the same gradient gives about 28 m/s.

blocks.title: Which way does it blow?
blocks.q: Over the United States, high pressure lies to the south and low pressure to the north. Which way does the wind blow aloft?
steps: Northern Hemisphere: low pressure on the wind's left.
If the low is to the north and on your left, you are facing east.
The wind blows toward the east: a west wind, the familiar westerlies.

blocks.html: Expecting upper winds to cross the isobars toward low pressure. Above the friction of the ground, the winds run along the isobars, with low pressure on the left in the Northern Hemisphere. Check: stand with your back to the wind aloft in the north, and the low is on your left.
Near the equator, $f$ is tiny, so the formula gives huge speeds and the balance breaks down. Geostrophic balance is a middle- and high-latitude idea.

blocks.html: Near the ground the wind is not quite geostrophic. Friction with trees, buildings and waves slows it, and that small change explains why lows bring clouds and highs bring clear skies, connecting to what lifts the air.

In the lowest kilometer, friction slows the wind, so the Coriolis force weakens and the wind crosses the isobars at an angle toward low pressure. In the Northern Hemisphere air spirals counterclockwise and inward around a low and clockwise and outward around a high; in the Southern Hemisphere the turning is reversed. Air spiraling into a low rises, building clouds; air spiraling out of a high sinks, clearing the sky.

The Coriolis force grows with wind speed. When friction slows the wind, the Coriolis force shrinks, and the pressure gradient force wins a little, pulling the wind across the isobars toward the low at an angle, often 10° to 45°, more over rough land than over smooth water. Around a low, that means air converging toward the center. It can't pile up there or go down into the ground, so it rises, cools and forms clouds and rain. Around a high, air diverges at the surface, and air from above sinks to replace it, warming as it sinks and drying the sky.

blocks.cap: Near the ground: friction slows the parcel, so it crosses the isobars into the low. Switch the hemisphere to see the turning reverse.

blocks.title: Turning around a low
blocks.q: Which way does surface air circle a low-pressure center in Australia?
steps: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere, where moving air turns left.
Air heading in toward the low is turned left, which sets up a clockwise spin.
Clockwise and inward: the reverse of a Northern Hemisphere low.

blocks.title: Find the low
blocks.q: You are in Ohio with a steady wind blowing from the south. Roughly where is the nearest low?
steps: Buys Ballot's law: in the Northern Hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind and the low is on your left (a little ahead).
Back to a south wind, you face north; your left is west.
The low lies to the west, a little to the north: weather in the west is coming your way.

blocks.html: Mixing up the turning directions. In the Northern Hemisphere: counterclockwise into a low, clockwise out of a high. In the Southern Hemisphere: clockwise into a low, counterclockwise out of a high. Check with the rule that moving air turns right in the north: air heading inward toward a low, turned right, ends up going around counterclockwise.

blocks.html: The Sun heats the tropics far more than the poles (sun angle), and the atmosphere carries the extra heat poleward. Put that together with rising air in lows and sinking air in highs and the Coriolis turn, and you get the planet-wide pattern of rain belts, deserts and prevailing winds.

In each hemisphere, three loops of circulation carry heat poleward. In the Hadley cell, air rises near the equator, flows poleward high up, and sinks near 30° latitude. In the Ferrel cell (30° to 60°), surface air flows poleward; in the polar cell, cold air sinks at the pole and flows toward 60°. Rising air makes the rainy belts near the equator and near 60°; sinking air makes the dry belts near 30° and at the poles. Coriolis turns the surface flows into the trade winds (0–30°), the westerlies (30–60°) and the polar easterlies.

Near the equator, strongly heated air rises in a band of towering clouds and heavy rain, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). High up, that air spreads poleward and cools by giving off infrared, and it is turned eastward by the Coriolis effect, so it piles up and sinks around 30°. Sinking air warms by compression and its relative humidity drops, so clouds can't form: the subtropical highs and the great deserts (the Sahara, the Arabian, the Kalahari, the Australian and the Sonoran) lie under them. Surface air returning toward the equator is turned right in the north and left in the south: the northeast and southeast trade winds.

blocks.cap: The three cells and the surface winds. Change the month: the rainy belt (ITCZ) follows the Sun, north in July and south in January, bringing wet and dry seasons to the tropics.

blocks.title: The winds at 15° S
blocks.q: Which way does the prevailing surface wind blow at 15° S?
steps: 15° S is in the Hadley cell, where surface air flows back toward the equator: northward.
In the Southern Hemisphere, moving air turns left. Air moving north turned left heads northwest.
It blows from the southeast: the southeast trade winds.

blocks.title: Why is the Sahara dry?
blocks.q: The Sahara lies near 20–30° N. Use the cells to explain its dryness.
steps: Air that rose over the equator flows north high up and sinks around 30° N.
Sinking air warms about 10 °C per km and its relative humidity drops far below 100%.
Clouds can't form in sinking, warming air, so it seldom rains.
blocks.a: It sits under sinking air of the Hadley cell

blocks.html: Thinking the great deserts are hot and dry because they are close to the Sun. Every place on Earth is essentially the same distance from the Sun; the deserts near 30° are dry because air sinks there, warming and drying as it comes down. Check: the equator gets even more sunlight but is one of the rainiest places on Earth, because air rises there.

The pattern shifts with the seasons. The ITCZ follows the high Sun, moving north in the northern summer and south in the southern summer. Over South Asia that shift, strengthened by the hot land, reverses the winds: moist ocean air flows in for the summer monsoon rains, and dry winds blow out from the land in winter.

blocks.html: Between the cells of the global circulation, where cold polar air meets warmer air from the south, the westerlies aloft become a narrow, fast river of wind: the jet stream. It is the geostrophic wind at its strongest.

The polar jet stream blows from west to east about 9 to 12 km up, above the boundary between polar and warmer air, often faster than 160 km/h (100 mph), and fastest in winter. It does not run straight: it meanders in great waves. Under a trough (a southward dip) the weather is cool and often stormy; under a ridge (a northward bulge) it is warm and settled. Storms tend to form and travel along the jet.

Cold air is denser and more compressed than warm air, so pressure drops faster with height over cold air than over warm air. Climb to airliner height and the pressure over the warm side is much higher than over the cold side at the same altitude. That big pressure difference over a short distance drives a strong geostrophic wind, with low pressure (the cold side) on its left: a west wind. The sharper the temperature contrast, the faster the jet, which is why it is strongest in winter, when the difference between the tropics and the poles is greatest.

blocks.cap: The jet streams seen from above the North Pole. Troughs carry cold air south; ridges carry warm air north. Change the number of waves to see different patterns.

blocks.title: Riding the jet
blocks.q: A jet flies 4200 km from Los Angeles to New York at an airspeed of 900 km/h, with a 150 km/h tailwind from the jet stream. How long does it take? How long would the return take against the same wind?
steps: Eastbound ground speed: $900 + 150 = 1050$ km/h; time $4200 \div 1050 = 4$ h.
About an hour and a half longer flying west, which is why airlines plan routes around the jet.

blocks.title: Trough or ridge?
blocks.q: In January the jet stream dips far south over the eastern United States and bulges north over the West. Where is it likely to be unusually cold?
steps: A southward dip is a trough, which lets polar air flow south under it.
A northward bulge is a ridge, with warm air underneath.
Cold in the East (under the trough), mild in the West (under the ridge).

blocks.html: Picturing the jet stream as a steady, straight band. It meanders in waves that slowly drift and change shape, and the waves steer weather systems: cold and stormy under troughs, warm and settled under ridges. Check: a forecast map of the jet almost always shows wiggles, and the storms are near the troughs.
A second, subtropical jet blows higher (about 12 to 14 km) near 30° latitude, at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell.

blocks.html: The trade winds blow across the tropical Pacific from east to west. They push the warm surface water west, in the same way that winds drive the surface currents you met in Earth Science. Every few years that balance tips one way or the other, and weather shifts around the world.

In normal years the trades pile warm water in the western Pacific, and cold water wells up off South America. In El Niño the trades weaken, warm water spreads east, and the heavy rain shifts east with it. In La Niña the trades strengthen and the eastern Pacific gets even cooler. NOAA tracks the sea-surface temperature anomaly in the central Pacific (the Niño 3.4 region): about +0.5 °C or more for several months in a row is El Niño, about −0.5 °C or less is La Niña.

The ocean and the air push each other. Strong trade winds drag warm surface water west, which leaves the east cool; a cool east and a warm west strengthen the pressure difference that drives the trades: a loop that holds itself in place. If the trades falter, warm water sloshes east, the east warms, the pressure difference weakens, and the trades falter more. The same feedback runs the other way into La Niña. The cycle repeats irregularly, every 2 to 7 years. Because the tropical Pacific is so large, moving its warmest water and its rain belt shifts the jet streams and storm tracks far away.

blocks.name: es-ocean
blocks.cap: The tropical Pacific in El Niño: weak trade winds and warm water spread east. Switch to neutral and La Niña to compare the winds, the warm pool and the rain.

blocks.title: Is it El Niño?
blocks.q: The Niño 3.4 region's average temperature for a season is 27.9 °C, and its normal for that season is 26.7 °C. What is the anomaly, and which phase does it point to?
steps: Anomaly = value − normal = $27.9 - 26.7 = +1.2$ °C.
+1.2 °C is above +0.5 °C: El Niño conditions, if it lasts for several overlapping seasons.

blocks.title: A three-month average
blocks.q: Monthly Niño 3.4 anomalies are −0.4, −0.7 and −0.9 °C. What is their three-month average, and what does it suggest?
steps: At or below −0.5 °C: La Niña conditions.

blocks.html: Blaming El Niño for every odd season. El Niño tilts the odds: in winter it makes a wet southern United States and a mild northern tier more likely, for example. It does not cause any particular storm, and some El Niño winters turn out differently. Check the wording of NOAA's outlooks: they give probabilities, such as "a 50% chance of above-normal precipitation," not certainties.
