blocks.html: A surface weather map is built from hundreds of station reports, each drawn as a tiny symbol called a station model. In one glance it gives the temperature, the dew point, the pressure, the wind and the sky. U.S. maps give temperatures in °F and wind in knots (1 knot ≈ 1.15 mph).

Around the station circle: temperature at the upper left and dew point at the lower left; a three-digit pressure code at the upper right; the 3-hour pressure change at the lower right; the sky cover as the fraction of the circle filled in; the weather symbol to the left. The wind barb's staff points toward where the wind comes from; on its end, a pennant is 50 knots, a full barb 10 knots and a half barb 5 knots.

The pressure code saves space. Sea-level pressures almost always lie between about 950 and 1050 hPa, so the leading 9 or 10 can be left off: the code is the last three digits of the pressure in tenths of a hectopascal. To decode, put a decimal point before the last digit, then put 10 in front if the code is below 500, or 9 if it is 500 or more. The wind barb is drawn like an arrow's feathered tail: the staff starts at the station and points into the wind, the way a weathervane's arrow points.

blocks.name: es-weather-map
blocks.cap: A station model. Change the sliders and watch each part of the symbol change: the barb swings to the direction the wind comes from, and its feathers add up to the speed.

blocks.title: Decoding the pressure
blocks.q: Decode the pressure codes 084 and 986.
steps: 084: put the decimal before the last digit, 08.4. The code is below 500, so put 10 in front: 1008.4 hPa.
986: 98.6, and the code is 500 or more, so put 9 in front: 998.6 hPa.

blocks.title: Reading the wind
blocks.q: A station's barb has its staff pointing toward the northwest, with one full barb and one half barb. What is the wind?
steps: The staff points to where the wind comes from: the northwest.
Speed: one full barb (10 kt) plus one half barb (5 kt) = 15 knots.
A northwest wind at 15 kt, about 17 mph.

blocks.title: Encoding
blocks.q: A station measures 1023.7 hPa. What code goes at the upper right?
steps: In tenths: 10237. Keep the last three digits: 237.

blocks.html: Reading the wind barb as pointing where the wind goes. The staff points toward the direction the wind comes from, just like the name: a "north wind" comes from the north. Check: on a map, barbs around a Northern Hemisphere low should show air circling counterclockwise and slanting inward, which only works if you read the staffs as "from."

blocks.html: In Earth Science you met air masses, huge bodies of air with the temperature and moisture of the place where they formed. With stability in hand, you can now see how an air mass changes as it travels, and why the Great Lakes bury some towns in snow.

Air masses are named by their source: c (continental, dry) or m (maritime, humid), then P (polar, cold), T (tropical, warm) or A (arctic, very cold). Over North America: cP and cA from Canada and the Arctic, mP from the North Pacific and North Atlantic, mT from the Gulf of Mexico and the warm Atlantic, and cT from the deserts of Mexico and the Southwest in summer. As an air mass moves over new ground or water, it is modified from below.

Air is heated or cooled mostly from the ground up. Cold air moving over warmer water or land is warmed at the bottom, so its lowest layer becomes warm compared with the air above: unstable. Bubbles rise, carrying heat and moisture up, and clouds and showers form. Warm air moving over cold ground is chilled at the bottom: a stable layer forms, often with fog or low stratus. In lake-effect snow, frigid cP air crosses a lake that hasn't frozen yet. The lake heats and moistens the bottom of the air, the air becomes unstable, and bands of heavy snow form on the downwind shore.

blocks.name: es-weather-map
blocks.cap: A surface map: cold, dry air lies behind the cold front, and warm, humid air fills the warm sector between the fronts.

blocks.title: Will the lake make snow?
blocks.q: In December a lake's surface water is 6 °C, and the air 1.5 km up (at about 850 hPa) is −10 °C. Forecasters use a rule of thumb: lake-effect snow is likely when the lake is at least 13 °C warmer than the air at 850 hPa. Is it likely?
steps: Difference: $6 - (-10) = 16$ °C.
16 °C is more than 13 °C, so the air over the lake is unstable enough.
In fact, 16 °C over about 1.5 km is about 10.7 °C per km, faster than the dry rate (9.8): absolutely unstable.

blocks.title: Which shore?
blocks.q: A cold northwest wind blows across Lake Ontario. Which shore gets the lake-effect snow?
steps: The air picks up heat and moisture as it crosses the lake.
It drops the snow when it reaches land on the downwind side.
A northwest wind blows toward the southeast: the southeast shore.

blocks.html: Thinking an air mass keeps its properties forever. Crossing warm water, cold ground, mountains or deserts changes its temperature and moisture from below. Arctic air reaching Florida is much warmer than when it left Canada; Pacific air that crosses the Rockies arrives on the Plains much drier. Check: ask what the ground or water under the air is doing to its lowest layer.

blocks.html: A front is the boundary between two air masses. At a cold front, cold air advances and the warm air ahead of it is shoved upward, one of the four ways air is lifted. On a map it is a blue line with triangles pointing the way it moves. A station in its path records a sudden change.

A cold front is steep (rising roughly 1 km for every 50 to 100 km), so it lifts warm, humid air sharply into a narrow band of showers and thunderstorms. As it passes (Northern Hemisphere): the pressure falls, reaches its lowest and then jumps up; the wind shifts from south or southwest to west or northwest, often gusty; the temperature and dew point drop; and the skies clear behind it.

Cold air is denser, so it hugs the ground and plows under the warm air like a wedge, and friction near the ground makes the leading edge bunch up and steepen. Forced up a steep slope, the warm, humid air rises fast, often in unstable towers: cumulonimbus. Behind the front, the cold, dry air brings a lower dew point and higher pressure (dense air weighs more). The wind shift follows from the pressure pattern: the front lies in a trough of low pressure, and the winds turn as it passes.

blocks.name: es-weather-map
blocks.cap: A cross section through a cold front: a steep wedge of cold air lifts the warm air into towering storm clouds along a narrow band.

blocks.title: When will it arrive?
blocks.q: A cold front is 180 km west of a town and moving east at 30 km/h. When will it reach the town?
steps: Time = distance ÷ speed = $180 \div 30 = 6$ hours.

blocks.title: How deep is the cold air?
blocks.q: A cold front slopes 1 km up for every 80 km. How deep is the cold air 200 km behind the front at the ground?
steps: Height of the front above that point: $200 \div 80 = 2.5$ km.
So the cold air is about 2.5 km deep there.

blocks.title: Reading a weather record
blocks.q: A station records: 3 p.m.: 27 °C, dew point 20 °C, wind S, 1005 hPa. 5 p.m.: 26 °C, wind SW, 1003 hPa, thunderstorm. 7 p.m.: 18 °C, dew point 9 °C, wind NW gusting, 1009 hPa. When did the front pass?
steps: Before 5 p.m.: warm, humid, south winds, falling pressure: ahead of the front.
By 7 p.m.: much colder and drier, northwest wind, pressure up: behind the front.
It passed between 5 and 7 p.m., with the thunderstorm at its leading edge.

blocks.html: Expecting it to warm up after the storms pass. Behind a cold front comes the cold air mass: the temperature and dew point fall and the pressure rises, often with gusty northwest winds and clearing skies. Check: a falling dew point is the surest sign the front has passed.

blocks.html: At a warm front, warm air advances and cold air retreats. It looks like the mirror image of a cold front, but it behaves very differently. Its long, slow approach is written in the sky, in the clouds you can name. On a map it is a red line with half circles on the side it is moving toward.

A warm front slopes gently, rising roughly 1 km for every 200 km or more. Warm air glides up over the cold air ahead, so the clouds arrive in order, high to low: cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus, then nimbostratus, with a wide band of steady rain (or snow) ahead of the front. After it passes, the temperature and dew point rise, the wind shifts (in the north, from east or southeast to south or southwest) and the pressure stops falling.

The warm air is less dense, so it can't push the heavy cold air out of the way along the ground. Instead it rides up over it, on a long, shallow ramp. Rising slowly over a huge area, the warm air cools gently and evenly, making layered clouds, not towers. Because the ramp is so shallow, the first clouds appear far ahead of the front at the ground: cirrus at 8 to 10 km may show up 1,000 km or more ahead, a day or two before the rain.

blocks.name: es-clouds
blocks.cap: The clouds ahead of a warm front, in the order they arrive: cirrus, then cirrostratus, altostratus, and finally nimbostratus with steady rain.

blocks.title: How far ahead are the cirrus?
blocks.q: A warm front slopes 1 km up for every 200 km. How far ahead of the front at the ground is the frontal surface 9 km up, where cirrus form?
steps: Distance = height × 200 = $9 \times 200 = 1800$ km.
The cirrus overhead can be 1,800 km ahead of the front at the ground.

blocks.title: When will it arrive?
blocks.q: Cirrostratus spread over a town when the warm front is 900 km away, moving at 25 km/h. How long until the front passes?
steps: Time = $900 \div 25 = 36$ hours: a day and a half of thickening clouds and then rain first.

blocks.html: Thinking warm air shoves the cold air away along the ground. The cold air is denser; the warm air rides up over it on a gentle slope, and the cold air slowly retreats. That is why warm-front weather arrives aloft first (high clouds) and spreads slowly, rather than hitting at once like a cold front. Check: steady rain for many hours points to a warm front; a short, violent downpour to a cold front.

blocks.html: Cold and warm fronts are not separate creatures: they are the two arms of one storm, a mid-latitude cyclone (a low). These storms are born under the jet stream and bring most of the rain and snow outside the tropics. Each has a warm front and a cold front.

A mid-latitude cyclone grows, matures and dies over a few days. It starts as a kink on a stationary front, deepens into an open wave with a warm front ahead and a cold front behind, matures as its pressure drops and winds strengthen, then occludes when the faster cold front catches the warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground. Cut off from warm, humid air, the low then fills and fades.

The storm feeds on the contrast between cold and warm air. As the low deepens, warm air flows north ahead of it (the warm front) and cold air flows south behind it (the cold front), turning stored temperature contrast into wind. A trough in the jet stream helps: air spreading apart aloft above the low pulls more air up from below, deepening it. Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts, so the cold front closes the gap. Once the warm air is lifted off the ground everywhere near the center, the fuel is cut off: occlusion marks the beginning of the end.

blocks.name: es-weather-map
blocks.cap: The life of a mid-latitude storm. Step through the stages: stationary front, wave, open wave, mature storm, occlusion, and decay.

blocks.title: Put the stages in order
blocks.q: Order these stages: occluded front, kink on a stationary front, open wave with a warm sector, the low fills and fades.
steps: Birth: a kink on a stationary front.
Growth: an open wave with a warm sector between the fronts.
Late life: the cold front catches the warm front: occlusion.
Death: the low fills and fades.

blocks.title: When will it occlude?
blocks.q: A storm's cold front moves 40 km/h and its warm front 25 km/h in the same direction, 450 km apart. About how long until the cold front catches up?
steps: The gap closes at $40 - 25 = 15$ km/h.
Time: $450 \div 15 = 30$ hours.

blocks.html: Thinking an occluded front means the storm is just forming. Occlusion comes late in a storm's life, when the cold front has caught the warm front; the low is usually at its deepest then and soon weakens. Check: the map symbol for an occluded front (purple, with triangles and half circles on the same side) sits near the center of a mature low, never at the start of a new one.
Map symbols: a stationary front alternates red half circles and blue triangles on opposite sides; an occluded front is purple with both shapes on the same side.

blocks.html: Now put it together: station models, isobars, highs and lows, and the fronts of a mid-latitude storm. A forecaster reads a surface map like a story about to happen.

On a surface map, isobars are drawn every 4 hPa around H and L centers. Winds circle lows counterclockwise and highs clockwise (Northern Hemisphere), crossing the isobars toward the low, strongest where the isobars crowd. Rain falls near the low and along its fronts. In the middle latitudes, the whole pattern usually travels from west to east, steered by the winds aloft, often 500 to 1,000 km a day.

The map shows forces and motion together. Isobar spacing tells you the pressure gradient, and so the wind speed. Friction and Coriolis tell you the direction: counterclockwise and inward around a low. Converging air at the low and lifting along fronts tell you where the clouds and rain are. And because the jet stream blows from the west, systems drift east: the weather to your west is a preview of your weather.

blocks.name: es-weather-map
blocks.cap: A surface map. Tap a spot to read its wind and what is coming; move the time slider forward to watch the low and its fronts travel east.

blocks.title: A forecast from the map
blocks.q: A town in Missouri has a low 600 km to its west, with a cold front trailing south of the low. The system moves east at 40 km/h. What happens over the next day?
steps: The low reaches the town's longitude in about $600 \div 40 = 15$ hours.
Before then, southerly winds bring warm, humid air; pressure falls.
As the cold front passes: a band of storms, a wind shift to the northwest, then colder, drier air and rising pressure.
blocks.a: Warm and humid, then storms, then colder

blocks.title: Counting isobars
blocks.q: The innermost isobar around a low is 996 hPa, and a town lies three isobars farther out. Isobars are drawn every 4 hPa. About what is the pressure at the town?
steps: Each isobar outward from a low is 4 hPa higher.
Three isobars: $996 + 3 \times 4 = 1008$ hPa.

blocks.title: The falling barometer
blocks.q: Near a town the pressure rises 2 hPa for every 100 km toward the east of an approaching low, and the pattern moves east at 50 km/h. About how fast does the town's barometer fall?
steps: Each hour the pattern moves 50 km, half of 100 km.
So the town's pressure drops by half of 2 hPa: about 1 hPa per hour.

blocks.html: Thinking weather moves at random. In the middle latitudes most systems travel from west to east, steered by the westerlies aloft, so the weather to the west is a good preview. Check: in a series of maps a day apart, the same low and fronts appear farther east each day.

blocks.html: A thunderstorm is unstable air let loose. Every thunderstorm needs three things, and you have met all of them: moisture, instability, and something to lift the air to its cloud base.

A thunderstorm grows from moisture (a high dew point), instability (surrounding air that cools fast with height) and a lift (heating, a front, a mountain or converging winds). A single storm passes through three stages: the cumulus stage (all updraft, the cloud towers upward), the mature stage (rain and a cold downdraft begin beside the updraft; lightning and the heaviest rain) and the dissipating stage (the downdraft takes over and cuts off the warm, moist air). A single storm often lives less than an hour.

Once lifted to its cloud base, a parcel in unstable air is warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising; condensation releases latent heat that keeps it warmer still. The updraft builds a tower up to the top of the troposphere, often 10 to 15 km, where the rising air spreads out into the flat anvil. Meanwhile droplets and ice grow big enough to fall. Falling rain drags air down with it, and some of the rain evaporates into drier air, chilling it; cold air is dense, so it plunges: the downdraft. When the downdraft spreads under the whole storm, it chokes off the updraft's supply of warm, humid air, and the storm dies.

blocks.name: es-storms
blocks.cap: A thunderstorm in its mature stage: the updraft feeds the tower and anvil while rain-cooled air rushes down and spreads out along the ground as a gust front. Step through the three stages.

blocks.title: Riding the updraft
blocks.q: A storm's updraft rises at 10 m/s from a cloud base at 1.5 km to a top at 12 km. How long does the air take to rise from base to top?
steps: Time: $10{,}500 \div 10 = 1050$ s, about 17.5 minutes.

blocks.title: Why is the top flat?
blocks.q: Why does a mature thunderstorm spread into a flat anvil near 12 km?
steps: Above the troposphere lies the stratosphere, where temperature stops falling with height and starts rising.
That layer is extremely stable: a rising parcel there is soon colder than its surroundings.
So the updraft stops rising and spreads sideways: the anvil.
blocks.a: The stable stratosphere acts as a lid

blocks.html: Thinking a storm's cold downdraft is wind blowing down from high above. It starts inside the storm: falling rain and hail drag air down, and rain evaporating into the drier air beneath the cloud chills it, making it dense enough to plunge. That is why the gust of cool air and the sharp drop in temperature arrive just before the heavy rain. Check: the air in a downdraft is rain-cooled, so the temperature falls as the outflow arrives.

Storms that live much longer than an hour, like squall lines and supercells, keep their updrafts and downdrafts apart, often because the wind changes with height. Supercells are the subject of the tornado lesson.

blocks.html: Inside a mature thunderstorm, collisions between ice particles separate electric charge, until the charge jumps as lightning. The thunder that follows lets you measure how far away the flash was, using unit rates.

Lightning heats a channel of air to around 30,000 °C in a fraction of a second. The air expands so violently that it makes a shock wave, which we hear as thunder. Light arrives almost instantly, but sound travels about 343 m/s, so each 3 seconds between flash and thunder is about 1 km (about 5 seconds per mile).

In the cold upper part of the storm, small ice crystals and soft hail pellets (graupel) collide in the strong updraft. Each collision passes a little charge: the light crystals, carried up, end up mostly positive; the heavier graupel, lower down, mostly negative. Charge builds until the air between can no longer hold it apart, and a spark tens of kilometers long jumps between the cloud and the ground or within the cloud. Distance from the delay is a rate problem: light covers a kilometer in about 3 millionths of a second, so all of the delay is the sound's travel time.

blocks.name: es-storms
blocks.cap: Count the seconds from flash to thunder: 9 s × 343 m/s ≈ 3.1 km. Change the delay to see the distance.

blocks.title: How far away?
blocks.q: You see a flash and count 12 seconds before the thunder. How far away was the lightning?
steps: Distance = speed × time = $343 \times 12 = 4116$ m.
About 4.1 km (or with the shortcut, $12 \div 3 = 4$ km; in miles, $12 \div 5 \approx 2.4$ mi).

blocks.title: Is it coming closer?
blocks.q: At 3:00 p.m. the delay is 15 s; at 3:10 p.m. it is 6 s. Estimate how fast the storm is approaching, using 3 s per km.
steps: At 3:00: $15 \div 3 = 5$ km away. At 3:10: $6 \div 3 = 2$ km away.
It came 3 km closer in 10 minutes ($\tfrac{1}{6}$ hour).
Speed: $3 \div \tfrac{1}{6} = 18$ km/h, toward you.

blocks.html: Believing lightning never strikes the same place twice. Lightning strikes tall, pointed and isolated objects again and again; the Empire State Building is struck more than 20 times in a typical year, according to the National Weather Service. Check: a place that was struck once is still tall and still exposed, so nothing protects it from the next strike.
Thunder can be heard about 15 km away or a little more, and lightning can strike that far from the storm. The National Weather Service's advice is short: "When thunder roars, go indoors."

blocks.html: Most thunderstorms never make a tornado. The ones that do are usually supercells: long-lived storms whose whole updraft rotates. The rotation comes from the wind itself, changing with height.

When the wind changes speed or direction with height (wind shear), the air near the ground rolls like a pencil between your hands. A strong updraft tilts that roll upright, and the storm's updraft starts to rotate: a mesocyclone, the mark of a supercell. A few supercells then produce a tornado, a violently rotating column of air touching the ground. Tornadoes are rated after they pass, from the damage they did, on the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, EF0 to EF5.

Shear makes spin: if the wind 1 km up blows much faster than the wind at the ground, the air between rolls over, making invisible horizontal tubes of spin. The updraft lifts the middle of a tube, bending it into an upside-down U with one rotating column on each side; one of them is drawn into the updraft. A rotating updraft lasts longer and grows stronger, because shear also keeps the downdraft from smothering it. Why some supercells make tornadoes and others don't is still an active research question.

blocks.title: Rate the tornado
blocks.q: A damage survey estimates a tornado's strongest gusts at 145 mph. What is its EF rating?
steps: EF3 covers 136 to 165 mph.
145 mph is in that range: EF3.

blocks.q: Another survey estimates 190 km/h. Convert to mph (1 mph ≈ 1.609 km/h) and rate it.
steps: $190 \div 1.609 \approx 118$ mph.
118 mph falls in 111–135: EF2.

blocks.html: Thinking tornadoes avoid cities, rivers, lakes or valleys. Tornadoes have crossed all of them, including the downtowns of large cities and wide rivers. Cities seem to be hit less often only because they cover a small share of the land. Check: there is no known terrain that blocks a tornado.
The United States has more tornadoes than any other country, about 1,200 in a typical year (NOAA).

blocks.html: A hurricane is a giant engine that runs on latent heat. It is made of thunderstorms organized into spiral bands around a calm eye, and it spins because of the Coriolis effect.

Hurricanes form over warm ocean water, about 26.5 °C (80 °F) or warmer, at least about 5° from the equator. Warm water evaporates into the air; when the vapor condenses in the storm's towering eyewall clouds, it releases latent heat that warms the core, lowers the pressure and strengthens the winds, which evaporate more water. They spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. The Saffir–Simpson category (1 to 5) rates only the maximum sustained wind.

The loop feeds itself: stronger winds over warm water mean more evaporation, which means more latent heat released aloft, a warmer core, lower surface pressure and stronger winds. The storm weakens when it loses its fuel: moving over cooler water or land, or into strong winds aloft that tear its tower apart. It needs the Coriolis effect to start spinning, which is why hurricanes almost never form near the equator, where the Coriolis effect is zero. In the eye, air sinks and warms, so the sky can clear.

steps: It is in the Southern Hemisphere, where air flowing in toward the low turns left.
Air spiraling into a southern low circles clockwise.

blocks.html: Judging a hurricane's danger by its category alone. The category measures only the wind. Storm surge (sea water pushed ashore by the wind) and flooding from heavy rain cause most hurricane deaths in the United States, and a slow, "weak" Category 1 storm can bring a deadly surge or rainfall. Check the forecasts for surge and rain, not just the category.

blocks.html: A thermometer gives the air's temperature, but your body cares how fast it loses heat. Wind carries heat away faster; humid air slows the cooling of sweat, which ties back to relative humidity. The National Weather Service turns these effects into two "feels like" numbers.

Wind chill is the temperature that would cool exposed skin as fast in calm air as the real temperature does in the wind. The heat index is how hot it feels when humidity slows the evaporation of sweat. Both are read from NWS charts in °F and mph. Wind chill applies at 50 °F or below with winds over 3 mph; the heat index is figured for shade, and full sunshine can raise it by up to about 15 °F.

Your body is warmer than cold air around it and loses heat into it. In still air, a thin layer of warmed air clings to your skin and insulates it; wind strips that layer away, so heat flows out faster: it feels colder. In heat, your body cools mainly by evaporating sweat, which takes latent heat from your skin. In humid air (a high dew point), sweat evaporates slowly, so you cool less: it feels hotter. Neither effect changes the air's real temperature.

blocks.q: The air is 38 °F with a 25 mph wind, and the wind chill is 27 °F. Can the wind make the water in a parked car's radiator freeze?
steps: Wind only speeds up cooling toward the air temperature.
A parked car makes no heat of its own, so the wind brings it down to 38 °F and no lower.
No: 38 °F is above freezing, so the wind can't freeze the water.

blocks.html: Thinking wind chill lowers the temperature of things. Wind makes warm objects lose heat faster, but it can only bring them down to the air temperature, never below it. A car, a water pipe or a thermometer in the wind settles at the air's temperature, not the wind chill. Check: wind chill matters for people and animals, which make their own heat.

blocks.html: Every number in a station model comes from an instrument. Thousands of stations, ships, buoys, aircraft and weather balloons measure the air at the same moments around the world, and those numbers are the starting point for every forecast.

A thermometer measures air temperature (in a shaded, ventilated shelter about 1.5 to 2 m above the ground); a barometer, air pressure; a hygrometer, humidity or dew point; a cup anemometer, wind speed; a wind vane, wind direction; a rain gauge, precipitation. A radiosonde, carried by a weather balloon, measures temperature, humidity and pressure (and, tracked by GPS, the wind) from the ground to about 30 km.

Each instrument is designed to measure the air itself, not something else. A thermometer in sunshine would measure sunlight on its own glass, so it sits in the shade with air flowing past it. A wind vane is a lopsided arrow: the wind pushes hardest on the big tail fin, swinging it downwind, so the arrowhead points into the wind, toward where it comes from. Balloon launches happen worldwide at the same two times each day (00 and 12 UTC), so forecasters get a snapshot of the whole atmosphere at one instant.

blocks.q: A rain gauge collects 1.25 inches of rain. How many millimeters is that? (1 inch = 25.4 mm)
steps: $1.25 \times 25.4 = 31.75$ mm, about 32 mm.

blocks.title: How long is a balloon flight?
blocks.q: A weather balloon rises about 5 m/s. How long does it take to reach 30 km, where it bursts?
steps: $6000 \div 60 = 100$ minutes, a little under two hours.

blocks.html: Thinking a wind vane points where the wind is going. It turns to point into the wind, toward the direction the wind comes from, which is how winds are named: a north wind blows from the north. Check: if smoke from a chimney drifts east, the vane on the roof points west.

blocks.html: Weather instruments at stations see only one spot. Satellites and radar see whole regions at once. Reading their images uses the ideas from sunlight in, infrared out.

Visible satellite images show sunlight reflected by clouds and the ground, so they go dark at night; thick clouds look brightest. Infrared images show the infrared each surface gives off, which tells its temperature; they work day and night, and they are usually drawn so that the coldest, highest cloud tops look brightest. Radar sends out microwave pulses and listens for echoes from raindrops, hail and snowflakes: it shows where precipitation is falling and how heavy it is, and Doppler radar also shows motion toward or away from the radar.

Clouds and the ground glow in the infrared, mostly near 10 μm, where the air is fairly transparent (the atmospheric window). A satellite measuring that glow can work out the temperature of whatever it sees: warm ground, or a cloud top. Since air cools with height, a colder top is a higher one, so a bright spot on an infrared image is a tall storm. Radar works the other way around: it makes its own signal. A pulse travels out at the speed of light, bounces off precipitation and comes back; the delay gives the distance, $d = ct/2$, and the strength of the echo gives the size and number of the drops. Cloud droplets are far too small to give a strong echo, which is why radar shows rain but not most clouds.

blocks.cap: The infrared glow of the ground (288 K) and of a cold storm top (220 K). Satellites read it through the window near 8 to 13 μm, where water vapor and CO₂ absorb little.

blocks.title: How far is the storm?
blocks.q: A radar pulse returns 0.6 milliseconds after it was sent. How far away is the rain? ($c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s)
steps: The pulse goes out and back, so the distance is half of $c \times t$.
The rain is about 90 km away.

blocks.title: How high is the cloud top?
blocks.q: An infrared satellite reads a cloud top at −55 °C. The ground is 25 °C, and the air cools about 6.5 °C per km. About how high is the top?
steps: Difference: $25 - (-55) = 80$ °C.
Height: $80 \div 6.5 \approx 12$ km: a towering thunderstorm.

blocks.html: Thinking satellite pictures show rain. Satellites mostly show clouds, and plenty of clouds produce no rain; radar shows where precipitation is actually falling. On an infrared image, remember the colors: the brightest clouds are the coldest, highest tops. Check: a visible image of the same storm at night is black, while the infrared image still shows it.

The U.S. radar network has about 160 Doppler radars (WSR-88D). The GOES weather satellites sit about 35,800 km above the equator, where an orbit takes exactly one day, so each one watches the same half of the planet all the time.

blocks.html: A forecaster reads surface maps and satellite images, but the backbone of every modern forecast is a computer model. Its strengths and limits come from one of the deepest ideas in science: chaos.

A numerical weather prediction model divides the atmosphere into a 3-D grid, starts from the observed state, and steps the laws of physics (motion, energy, water and gas laws) forward a few minutes at a time. Because tiny errors in the starting state grow over time (chaos), forecasts lose skill after several days. Forecasters run an ensemble: many runs from slightly different starting states. Where the runs agree, confidence is high; where they spread apart, it is low.

In 1963 Edward Lorenz found that a simple model of convection, restarted from numbers rounded in the fourth decimal place, soon gave a completely different "weather." Small differences grew, roughly doubling every so often, until they were as big as the weather itself. The real atmosphere behaves this way: no thermometer network can measure every gust, and even a perfect model would start from a slightly wrong picture. So instead of one forecast, models make many, and the share of runs that do something (say, rain) becomes a probability.

blocks.name: es-chance
blocks.cap: An ensemble: 30 runs of a toy chaotic model that start almost the same. They agree for the first days, then fan out. The share of members with rain on a day is the forecast chance of rain.

blocks.title: How many grid points?
blocks.q: A model covers the contiguous United States, about 8,000,000 km², with grid columns 10 km apart and 50 levels. About how many grid points is that?
steps: Each column covers $10 \times 10 = 100$ km², so there are $8{,}000{,}000 \div 100 = 80{,}000$ columns.
Times 50 levels: $80{,}000 \times 50 = 4{,}000{,}000$ grid points, each stepped forward thousands of times.

blocks.title: Errors that double
blocks.q: A forecast starts with a temperature error of 0.1 °C that doubles every 2 days. How big is it after 10 days?
steps: 10 days is 5 doublings.
$0.1 \times 2^5 = 0.1 \times 32 = 3.2$ °C, about as big as a real day-to-day change.

blocks.html: Thinking a missed forecast means forecasting doesn't work. Small errors grow with time, so forecasts are very good a day or two ahead, useful for about a week, and lose most of their skill beyond about 10 days. NOAA puts it this way: a 5-day forecast is right about 90% of the time and a 7-day forecast about 80%, while forecasts of 10 days or more are right only about half the time. Check: compare a 1-day forecast's record with a 10-day forecast's.

blocks.html: The forecast says "40% chance of rain." People read that in many ways, most of them wrong. The National Weather Service defines it precisely, and the definition connects to the ensemble forecasts you just met and to probability from math.

The probability of precipitation (PoP) is the chance that measurable precipitation (at least 0.01 inch, about 0.25 mm) falls at any given point in the forecast area during the forecast period. The National Weather Service computes it as $$\text{PoP} = C \times A$$ where $C$ is the forecaster's confidence that rain will occur somewhere in the area and $A$ is the fraction of the area expected to get it.

The forecast has to answer the question you care about: "will it rain where I am?" If a forecaster is sure it will rain ($C = 100\%$) but only on 40% of the area, your spot has a 40% chance. If she is only 50% sure rain will develop, but if it does it will cover 80% of the area, your chance is $0.5 \times 0.8 = 40\%$ again. Both forecasts say 40%, and both mean the same thing for you: in situations like this, rain falls at a given spot about 4 times in 10.

blocks.name: es-chance
blocks.cap: The share of ensemble members with rain on a day gives a chance of rain. Move the forecast day: the farther ahead, the more the members disagree.

blocks.title: Computing a PoP
blocks.q: A forecaster is 80% confident that showers will form, and expects them to cover half the county if they do. What PoP goes in the forecast?
steps: PoP = $0.8 \times 0.5 = 0.4$, a 40% chance of rain.

blocks.title: Checking the forecasts
blocks.q: Over a year, a forecaster gave a 30% chance of rain on 60 days. Rain fell on 19 of those days. Were the forecasts well calibrated?
steps: A 30% forecast should see rain on about 30% of such days: $0.3 \times 60 = 18$ days.
Rain fell on 19 days, very close to 18.
Yes: the 30% forecasts meant what they said. A day with 30% that turned rainy was not a "wrong" forecast.

blocks.html: Thinking a 40% chance means rain for 40% of the day, or over 40% of the area. It means a 4 in 10 chance that measurable rain falls at any given spot in the area during the period. Check: 40% of the area with full confidence and 80% of the area with half confidence give the same 40%.
The chance of staying dry is $1 - \text{PoP}$: a 40% chance of rain is a 60% chance of no measurable rain at your spot.

blocks.html: In Earth Science you learned that climate is the pattern of weather over 30 years or more. Meteorologists make that precise with climate normals, and they describe any day, month or year by how far it is from normal, using signed numbers.

A climate normal is a 30-year average of a weather element, for a date, month, season or year. NOAA's current U.S. normals cover 1991–2020 and are updated every ten years. An anomaly is a value minus its normal: $$\text{anomaly} = \text{value} - \text{normal}$$ Positive means above normal; negative, below.

One day's weather swings far more than climate does, so you need a long average to see what is typical: 30 years is long enough to smooth out odd years, short enough to describe the climate of today. Anomalies let you compare unlike places and seasons fairly. A 25 °C day is cool for Phoenix in July and hot for Seattle in March; their anomalies show it at once. Global temperature records are kept as anomalies for a deeper reason: the anomaly at a station far from the next one still tells the same regional story, even when their actual temperatures differ because of height or coastline.

blocks.name: es-climate-data
blocks.cap: A map of yearly temperature anomalies: each place compared with its own normal. Red is warmer than normal, blue cooler. A blue area can still be hot; it is just cooler than usual for that place.

blocks.title: A hot July day
blocks.q: The normal high for July 15 in a city is 88 °F. This July 15 the high was 95 °F. What was the anomaly?
steps: Anomaly = value − normal = $95 - 88 = +7$ °F.

blocks.title: A cold month
blocks.q: A town's January normal is −3.4 °C, and this January averaged −6.1 °C. What was the anomaly?
steps: January was 2.7 °C colder than normal.

blocks.html: Reading an anomaly map as a map of actual temperatures. A blue (negative) area in Arizona in July can still be over 40 °C, just a little cooler than its own normal; a red area in Antarctica is still far below freezing. Check the legend: an anomaly map is labeled in degrees above or below normal.

Changing the baseline period moves the zero line, not the trend. NASA reports global temperatures relative to 1951–1980; NOAA uses the 20th century; the IPCC uses 1850–1900. The same year gets different anomaly values, but the warming from decade to decade is the same in all three.

blocks.html: A climograph packs a place's climate normals into one picture: average temperature for each month as a line, and average precipitation for each month as bars. With practice you can read a climate from it at a glance.

From a climograph you can read the warmest and coldest months, the annual temperature range (warmest minus coldest), the total yearly precipitation (the sum of the bars) and when the wet and dry seasons come. If the warm months are December to February, the place is in the Southern Hemisphere.

Each feature of the graph comes from a cause you have studied. A small annual range means the ocean or the tropics (why coasts stay mild); a large one means the middle of a continent at high latitude. A summer peak of rain means rising air in summer (the shifting tropical rain belt, monsoons or thunderstorms); a winter peak means storms on the westerlies in winter, as on the west coasts in the middle latitudes. The Southern Hemisphere's seasons are reversed because the Sun is high there from November to February.

blocks.title: Reading Sydney
blocks.q: Sydney, Australia averages about 23.5 °C in January and 13 °C in July. What is its annual range, and what does the timing tell you?
steps: Range: $23.5 - 13 = 10.5$ °C, small, because Sydney is on the coast.
January is the warm month, so Sydney is in the Southern Hemisphere.

blocks.title: Wet season
blocks.q: A city's monthly precipitation (mm) from January to December is 0, 0, 0, 0, 15, 525, 840, 525, 340, 90, 15, 5. When is its wet season, and what is its yearly total?
steps: The rain is concentrated in June through September.
A wet summer and a long dry season: a monsoon climate like Mumbai's.

blocks.html: Assuming the warmest months are always June to August. In the Southern Hemisphere they are December to February: Sydney, Cape Town and Buenos Aires have summer at Christmas. Check which months are warmest before naming the seasons.

blocks.html: Put climographs side by side and patterns appear: places with similar latitudes and settings (what sets a place's climate) have similar climates. In 1900 Wladimir Köppen sorted the world's climates into groups by temperature and precipitation, partly from the plants that grow in each. Versions of his scheme are still the standard.

Köppen's five main groups: E, polar (warmest month below 10 °C); B, dry (yearly precipitation below a threshold that rises with temperature); A, tropical (coldest month 18 °C or warmer); C, temperate (coldest month between −3 °C and 18 °C); D, continental (coldest month −3 °C or colder, warmest at least 10 °C). Check them in that order: E, then B, then A, C or D. (Some U.S. books use 0 °C instead of −3 °C between C and D.)

Each line marks a change that plants and people notice. Trees need a warmest month of about 10 °C, so polar climates are treeless tundra and ice. Dryness depends on more than rainfall: hot places lose water to evaporation faster, so the dry threshold rises with the average temperature, about $20 \times (\text{mean temperature in °C}) + 280$ mm when most of the precipitation falls in summer (+140 when it is spread out, +0 when it falls mostly in winter). Below half the threshold the climate is desert (BW); between half and the full threshold, steppe (BS).

blocks.title: Classify a town
blocks.q: A town's warmest month is 24 °C and its coldest −8 °C. It averages 9 °C over the year and gets 800 mm of precipitation, about two thirds in summer. Which group?

steps: Warmest month is well above 10 °C, so not E.

blocks.html: Calling any hot place a desert. A desert is defined by too little precipitation for its temperature, not by heat: Singapore is hot and very wet, while Antarctica is so dry that it is the largest desert on Earth. Check the precipitation against the dry threshold, not the temperature alone.

blocks.html: Carbon dioxide is the gas at the center of the greenhouse effect, and the carbon in it is always on the move: through the air, the ocean, living things and rock. You met fossil fuels as resources that took millions of years to form; here you follow their carbon.

Carbon is stored in reservoirs: the air (about 900 billion tonnes of carbon, GtC, today), plants (about 450 GtC), soils (about 1,700 GtC), the ocean (about 38,000 GtC, mostly deep) and rocks (tens of millions of GtC). It moves between them in fluxes. The fast cycle runs through photosynthesis, respiration and the ocean surface, roughly a hundred GtC each way every year. The slow cycle runs through rock weathering, burial and volcanoes, well under 1 GtC a year. Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from the slow cycle into the fast one, about 10 GtC a year.

Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide from the air and builds sugar from it: $6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$. Respiration and decay run the reaction backward. These two huge fluxes nearly cancel each year, as do the ocean's uptake and release, so the amount in the air stayed nearly steady for thousands of years. The slow cycle was balanced too: volcanoes add a little carbon, and weathering and burial of shells remove a little. Fossil fuels are ancient plants and plankton whose carbon was buried out of the fast cycle for millions of years. Burning them returns that carbon in decades, much faster than the slow cycle can take it back.

blocks.cap: The carbon cycle: reservoirs as boxes and fluxes as arrows, in GtC and GtC per year (rounded, after the IPCC's carbon-cycle figures). Tap a reservoir or an arrow to read it.

blocks.title: How long does a carbon atom stay in the air?
blocks.q: The air holds about 900 GtC. About 120 GtC a year go into plants and about 80 GtC a year into the ocean. On average, how long does a carbon atom stay in the air before it is swapped out?
steps: Total flux out: $120 + 80 = 200$ GtC a year.
Average stay: $900 \div 200 = 4.5$ years.
But that is a swap: similar amounts come back each year. The extra carbon we add is removed far more slowly, over centuries to many thousands of years.

blocks.title: Where does a tree's mass come from?
blocks.q: In glucose, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$ (molar mass 180 g/mol), how many grams of every 180 g are carbon, and where did that carbon come from?
steps: Six carbon atoms at 12 g/mol: $6 \times 12 = 72$ g of the 180 g, which is 40%.
All of that carbon came from carbon dioxide in the air, through the leaves.
blocks.a: 72 g, from CO₂ in the air

blocks.html: Thinking plants get their mass from the soil. Nearly all of a plant's dry mass is built from carbon dioxide taken from the air, plus water; minerals from the soil are a few percent. Check: a tree that grows by a tonne does not leave a tonne-sized hole in the ground around it.
Volcanoes add only about 0.1 GtC a year. People now add roughly a hundred times as much (USGS).

blocks.html: People add about 11 billion tonnes of carbon to the carbon cycle each year. Where does it go? This is bookkeeping with numbers in scientific notation, and every number in it is measured independently.

About 2.124 GtC of carbon added to the air raises its carbon dioxide by 1 ppm. Of the carbon people emit, a little under half (about 45%, the airborne fraction) stays in the air; the ocean and the land take up the rest. So $$\Delta\text{CO}_2\ (\text{ppm}) \approx \frac{\text{emissions (GtC)} \times 0.45}{2.124}$$

Where does 2.124 come from? The atmosphere has a mass of about $5.1 \times 10^{18}$ kg, or about $1.8 \times 10^{20}$ moles of air. One ppm of that is $1.8 \times 10^{14}$ moles of CO₂, and each mole holds 12 g of carbon: about $2.1 \times 10^{15}$ g, which is 2.1 GtC. The sinks work because extra CO₂ in the air pushes more into the ocean (it dissolves) and speeds up plant growth. The Global Carbon Budget for 2013–2022 balances like this, in GtC a year: emissions from fossil fuels about 9.6 and from land-use change about 1.3; the air gained about 5.2, the ocean took about 2.8, and the land about 3.3.

blocks.name: es-carbon
blocks.cap: One year of human emissions (11 GtC): about 45% stays in the air, and the ocean and land take the rest. The readout turns the air's share into ppm.

blocks.title: One year's rise
blocks.q: Emissions are 11 GtC in a year, and 45% stays in the air. By how many ppm does CO₂ rise?
steps: Carbon staying in the air: $11 \times 0.45 = 4.95$ GtC.
In ppm: $4.95 \div 2.124 \approx 2.3$ ppm.
Close to the measured rise of about 2.4 ppm a year in the 2010s.

blocks.title: Tonnes of CO₂
blocks.q: Fossil-fuel emissions in 2023 were about 10.0 GtC. How many billion tonnes of CO₂ is that? (CO₂ has a mass of 44 for every 12 of carbon.)
steps: Each tonne of carbon becomes $44/12 \approx 3.67$ tonnes of CO₂ when it combines with oxygen.
$10.0 \times 3.67 \approx 36.7$ billion tonnes of CO₂.

blocks.html: Assuming all emitted carbon dioxide stays in the air. Measurements show only a little under half does; the ocean and land take up the rest, which is why the yearly rise in ppm is less than half what emissions alone would give ($11 \div 2.124 \approx 5.2$ ppm). The carbon the ocean takes is not gone: it makes seawater more acidic. Check: emissions ÷ 2.124 should be roughly twice the measured yearly rise.

blocks.html: In 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide on Mauna Loa in Hawaii, far from cities and forests. NOAA continues the record today. It is the most famous graph in climate science, and reading it uses average rate of change and the carbon budget.

The Mauna Loa record shows two things. A yearly wiggle of about 6 ppm, highest in May and lowest in September or October, from the growth and decay of northern plants. And a steady rise beneath it, from about 316 ppm in 1959 to about 425 ppm in 2024, rising faster over time: under 1 ppm a year in the 1960s, about 2.4 ppm a year in the 2010s. Before industry, the air held about 280 ppm.

Most land, and so most plants, is in the Northern Hemisphere. In the northern spring and summer, plants take in more carbon dioxide than they release, and the level falls; in fall and winter, decay and respiration win, and it climbs. The swing repeats every year. Underneath, the burning of fossil fuels adds more each year than the sinks remove, so each year's average is higher than the last. The rise speeds up because emissions grew over the decades.

blocks.title: Rate of change
blocks.q: Mauna Loa measured about 390 ppm in 2010 and about 414 ppm in 2020. What was the average rate of rise?
steps: Rate: $24 \div 10 = 2.4$ ppm per year.

blocks.title: Compared with before industry
blocks.q: By what percent had CO₂ risen above the pre-industrial 280 ppm when it reached 425 ppm?
steps: Increase: $425 - 280 = 145$ ppm.
Percent: $145 \div 280 \approx 0.52$, about a 52% increase.

blocks.html: Thinking the dip each spring and summer means the rise is reversing. The dip comes every year as northern plants grow, and it is followed by a rise to a new high. Compare the same month in different years, or yearly averages, to see the trend. Check: every yearly average in the Mauna Loa record is higher than the year before.

blocks.html: The energy balance sets Earth's temperature. Anything that changes the energy coming in or going out, measured in watts per square meter, pushes climate warmer or cooler. These pushes are called forcings; the rising carbon dioxide is the biggest one today.

A radiative forcing is a change in Earth's energy balance, in W/m²: positive warms, negative cools. Natural forcings include changes in sunlight and volcanic eruptions. Human forcings include greenhouse gases (positive), pollution particles called aerosols (mostly negative: they reflect sunlight and brighten clouds) and land-cover changes. By 2019 the total human forcing since 1750 was about +2.7 W/m²; changes in the Sun over that time add almost nothing (IPCC 2021).

Think of Earth's energy budget as income (absorbed sunlight) and spending (infrared to space). More greenhouse gas lowers the spending until Earth warms enough to restore the balance. More reflective haze or brighter clouds cut the income. A big volcanic eruption that reaches the stratosphere makes a haze of sulfuric acid droplets that reflects sunlight for a year or two; then it settles out. That is why a volcano gives a short, sharp cooling, while long-lived carbon dioxide gives a lasting push.

blocks.html: Thinking a big volcanic eruption warms the climate. Its gases do include carbon dioxide, but far less than people emit; the big effect is the sulfur haze in the stratosphere, which reflects sunlight and cools Earth for a year or two. Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991 and cooled the global average by about half a degree Celsius in 1992. Check the sign: volcanic forcing is negative.

blocks.html: A forcing starts a change in temperature, but the climate answers back. Some responses make the change bigger, some make it smaller. These are feedbacks, and they decide how much Earth finally warms.

A positive feedback strengthens the change that caused it; a negative feedback weakens it. The strongest negative feedback is Earth's own glow: a warmer planet gives off more infrared ($\sigma T^4$). Positive feedbacks include water vapor (warmer air holds more of this greenhouse gas) and ice and snow albedo (melting uncovers darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight). Cloud feedbacks are probably positive overall, but less certain.

Each feedback is measured in W/m² per degree of warming. The IPCC's best estimates: Earth's extra glow, about −3.2; water vapor (with the change in how temperature falls with height), about +1.3; ice and snow albedo, about +0.35; clouds, about +0.4. The net is about −1.15 W/m² per °C: still negative, so the climate settles, but much less negative than the glow alone. Warming at balance = forcing ÷ (minus the net feedback). With only Earth's glow, doubling carbon dioxide (+3.7 W/m²) would warm about $3.7/3.2 \approx 1.2$ °C; with all the feedbacks, about $3.7/1.15 \approx 3.2$ °C.

blocks.title: Ice and albedo
blocks.q: Warming melts sea ice and uncovers dark ocean. Is this a positive or negative feedback?
steps: The ocean absorbs much more sunlight than ice (lower albedo).
More absorbed sunlight means more warming, which melts more ice.
The change strengthens itself: a positive feedback.

blocks.title: Warming with feedbacks
blocks.q: A forcing of +3.7 W/m² acts on a climate whose net feedback is −1.5 W/m² per °C. How much does Earth warm at balance?
steps: Warming = forcing ÷ (minus the net feedback) = $3.7 \div 1.5$.
$\approx 2.5$ °C.

blocks.html: Thinking a positive feedback is a good thing. In science, "positive" means only that the change strengthens itself, whatever its effects; "negative" means it weakens itself. Melting ice speeding up warming is a positive feedback even though few would call it good. Check: ask whether the response pushes in the same direction as the original change.

blocks.html: For the last million years, great ice sheets have grown over North America and Europe and melted away again, over and over. The pacemaker is Earth's orbit, and the feedbacks you just met turn its gentle nudges into ice ages.

Three slow cycles change how sunlight is spread over Earth's seasons and latitudes (the Milankovitch cycles): the shape of the orbit (eccentricity, about 100,000 and 400,000 years), the tilt of the axis (between about 22.1° and 24.5°, every 41,000 years) and the direction the axis points (precession, which shifts the date of closest approach to the Sun, about every 19,000 to 23,000 years). Ice ages have come and gone about every 100,000 years for the last 800,000 years.

The cycles barely change the total sunlight Earth gets in a year, but they shift it between seasons and latitudes. What matters most is summer sunlight far north, near 65° N, where the great ice sheets grow: when northern summers are weak (less tilt, and the far point of the orbit falling in northern summer), winter snow survives the summer and ice builds up year after year. Feedbacks then amplify the change: growing ice reflects more sunlight, and the colder ocean takes up carbon dioxide, which cools Earth further. Ice-core records show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together through every cycle.

blocks.cap: The orbital cycles. Change the orbit's shape, the tilt and the date of closest approach, and watch the summer sunlight at 65° N rise and fall.

blocks.title: Closest and farthest
blocks.q: Today Earth is about 147.1 million km from the Sun in early January and 152.1 million km in early July. How much stronger is the sunlight in January?
steps: Sunlight weakens as 1/distance², so the ratio is $(152.1/147.1)^2$.
$152.1/147.1 \approx 1.034$, and $1.034^2 \approx 1.07$: about 7% stronger in January.
The seasons are still set by the tilt, not the distance: January is winter in the north.

blocks.title: Counting cycles
blocks.q: How many tilt cycles (41,000 years each) fit into one 100,000-year ice-age cycle?
steps: The cycles overlap and combine, which is why ice ages are irregular in shape.

blocks.html: Thinking orbital cycles explain today's warming. They act over tens of thousands of years, and the orbital pattern today would, on its own, cool Earth very slowly. The warming since 1900 has happened in about a century and is matched by the measured rise in greenhouse gases. Check the time scales: about 5 °C of warming at the end of the last ice age took roughly 10,000 years; about 1.1 °C of warming since the late 1800s has taken about 150.

blocks.html: Thermometers go back only about 150 years worldwide. To test ideas like the orbital cycles, scientists read climate from natural records called proxies: layers that build up year by year and keep a chemical memory of the climate when they formed.

Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica hold bubbles of ancient air (a direct sample of past carbon dioxide and methane), and the oxygen in the ice records past temperature; Antarctic cores reach back about 800,000 years. Tree rings record growing conditions year by year, for thousands of years. Ocean sediment cores hold the shells of tiny plankton whose chemistry records ocean temperature and ice volume over millions of years. Corals, cave formations and pollen add more records.

Many proxies are layered, so they can be counted like pages: one tree ring or one band of ice for each year, where snow or growth changes with the seasons. Their chemistry acts as a thermometer. Water molecules with the heavier oxygen-18 atom evaporate a little less easily and condense a little more easily, so by the time vapor reaches the poles in a cold climate, more of the heavy oxygen has already rained out, and polar snow is "lighter." Bubbles trapped as snow turns to ice seal in samples of the air itself. Records from different proxies, places and methods agree with each other, which is what makes them trustworthy.

blocks.title: Counting layers
blocks.q: A Greenland ice core has yearly layers about 2.5 cm thick near the top. About how many years does the top 50 m cover?
steps: $5000 \div 2.5 = 2000$ layers: about 2000 years.
Deeper down the layers are squeezed thinner, so the same length of core covers more years.

blocks.title: Then and now
blocks.q: Through the last 800,000 years, ice cores show carbon dioxide between about 180 ppm (ice ages) and 300 ppm (warm times). Today it is about 425 ppm. How much higher is today than the highest level in the cores?
steps: As a percentage of 300: $125 \div 300 \approx 42\%$ higher.
The IPCC (2021) concluded that carbon dioxide is now higher than at any time in at least 2 million years.

blocks.html: Thinking we know past climates only from written records. Writing covers a few thousand years at most, and thermometers about 150 years worldwide; bubbles in Antarctic ice hold samples of air from about 800,000 years ago, and ocean sediments reach back tens of millions of years. Check: ask what a record is made of, and how its layers are dated.

blocks.html: How much warmer will Earth get if carbon dioxide doubles? This number, the climate sensitivity, combines the forcing from carbon dioxide with all the feedbacks. Because the forcing grows with the logarithm of the concentration, the math uses logarithms.

The forcing from carbon dioxide grows with the logarithm of its concentration: $$\Delta F = 5.35\,\ln\frac{C}{C_0}\ \text{W/m}^2$$ so each doubling adds the same push, about 3.7 W/m² by this formula (the IPCC's latest assessment puts it near 3.9). The equilibrium climate sensitivity, the eventual warming per doubling, is likely 2.5 to 4 °C, with a best estimate of 3 °C (IPCC 2021). So the eventual warming is about $S \times \log_2(C/C_0)$.

Why a logarithm? Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared strongly near the center of its absorption band, so the center is already "full": adding more there changes little. Extra carbon dioxide mainly widens the band at its edges, where absorption is weaker, and that widening grows more slowly with each addition. The result is that each doubling, 280 to 560 ppm or 560 to 1120 ppm, adds about the same forcing. The warming arrives slowly: the deep ocean takes centuries to warm, so the warming at any moment lags behind the eventual (equilibrium) warming.

blocks.cap: Forcing from carbon dioxide compared with 280 ppm. Drag the point: 560 ppm gives about 3.7 W/m², and 1120 ppm about 7.4, double the push for four times the gas.

blocks.title: One doubling
blocks.q: Carbon dioxide goes from 280 to 560 ppm. With a sensitivity of 3 °C per doubling, what is the eventual warming?
steps: $560/280 = 2$: exactly one doubling, $\log_2 2 = 1$.
Warming: $3 \times 1 = 3$ °C.

blocks.title: Where we are now
blocks.q: Carbon dioxide was about 425 ppm in 2024, compared with 280 ppm before industry. How many doublings is that, and what eventual warming does it imply at 3 °C per doubling? ($\log_2 1.52 \approx 0.60$)
steps: $425/280 \approx 1.52$, and $\log_2 1.52 \approx 0.60$ doublings.
Eventual warming from CO₂ alone: $3 \times 0.60 \approx 1.8$ °C.
The measured warming is so far about 1.1 to 1.3 °C, smaller because the ocean is still catching up and aerosols mask part of it.

blocks.html: Expecting each added ppm to warm by the same amount. The push grows with the logarithm of the concentration, so going from 280 to 560 ppm warms about as much as going from 560 to 1120. Check: equal ratios give equal forcing: $5.35\ln 2 \approx 3.7$ W/m² for any doubling.

blocks.html: As Earth warms (what changes climate), the oceans rise for two reasons. Satellites have measured the global sea level since 1993, and tide gauges go back much further.

Sea level rises because seawater expands as it warms, and because ice on land (glaciers and the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets) melts or slides into the sea. Global mean sea level rose about 20 cm from 1901 to 2018, and about 10 cm since 1993 alone, at a rate that has more than doubled (IPCC 2021; NASA). Melting sea ice, which already floats, adds almost nothing.

Water, like most materials, takes up more space when warmer: seawater expands by roughly 0.01 to 0.03% for each degree, depending on its temperature. Spread over an ocean thousands of meters deep, that adds up. Land ice is new water for the ocean: when it melts or flows into the sea, the ocean gains that water. Floating ice is different. By Archimedes' principle, floating ice already pushes aside its own weight of water, so when it melts it fills almost exactly the hole it made. Since 1971, about half of the rise has come from warming water and most of the rest from melting glaciers and ice sheets (IPCC 2021).

blocks.cap: Global mean sea level since 1993 from satellites (a smooth curve fitted to NASA's record): about 10 cm of rise, getting steeper.

blocks.title: A melting ice cap
blocks.q: An ice cap on land holds 1000 km³ of ice (density 0.917 g/cm³). If it all melted, about how much would global sea level rise? The ocean covers about 361,000,000 km².
steps: Water from the ice: $1000 \times 0.917 = 917$ km³.
Spread over the ocean: $917 \div 361{,}000{,}000 \approx 2.54 \times 10^{-6}$ km.
That is about 2.5 mm. Greenland's ice, about 2.9 million km³, would add about 7 m.

blocks.title: Warming water
blocks.q: The top 700 m of the ocean warms by 0.5 °C, and seawater expands by 0.0002 of its height per °C. About how much does sea level rise?
steps: Rise = depth × expansion per °C × warming = $700 \times 0.0002 \times 0.5$.
$= 0.07$ m, about 7 cm.

blocks.html: Thinking melting sea ice raises sea level. Sea ice already floats, displacing its own weight of water, so melting it barely changes the level, just as melting ice cubes don't make a full glass overflow. Only ice that sits on land (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctica) adds water to the ocean. Check: ask whether the ice is floating or resting on land.

Projected rise by 2100 (compared with 1995–2014) is likely about 0.3 to 0.6 m if emissions are cut deeply and about 0.6 to 1.0 m with very high emissions (IPCC 2021). The rise continues for centuries, because the deep ocean and the ice sheets respond slowly.

blocks.html: If weather forecasts lose skill after about ten days, how can scientists say anything about 2100? Because they are answering a different question. Climate projections use the climate sensitivity and the same physics as weather models, but they predict long-term averages.

A climate model uses the same laws of physics as a weather model, run on a coarser grid for decades or centuries, with the ocean, ice and land included. It projects the statistics of weather (averages, ranges, extremes) for a given path of future emissions, called a scenario, not the weather on any particular date. Global surface temperature in 2011–2020 was about 1.1 °C above 1850–1900; by 2081–2100 it is projected to be about 1.4 °C above with very low emissions and about 4.4 °C above with very high emissions (best estimates, IPCC 2021).

Weather is chaotic: the exact sequence of storms depends on tiny details of the starting state. Climate is the average of weather, and the average is set by the energy balance, which depends on the forcings, not on the starting details. A coin toss is unpredictable, but the share of heads in 10,000 tosses is not; a die can be loaded so that sixes come up more often, even if no single roll can be predicted. Climate models are tested by running them over the past: they reproduce the measured warming of the last century only when the human forcings are included.

blocks.title: Coins and climate
blocks.q: A fair coin is tossed 10,000 times. You can't predict any single toss. About how many heads do you expect, and how sure can you be?
steps: Expected: $0.5 \times 10{,}000 = 5000$ heads.
Almost every run of 10,000 tosses lands within about 100 of 5000 (within 2 standard deviations, $2\sqrt{10{,}000 \times 0.25} = 100$).
The single toss is like weather; the share of heads is like climate.
